  • Appendix A: Changelog
    • Unreleased

hash is one entry point for hashing and key derivation in a C++20 program, on every target webcpp has, one of the libraries of webcpp. The algorithms are Boost.Hash2’s and those of C libraries, each a backend that the program names in its own Jamfile.

This page is written for two readers at once: a developer who knows little cryptography and wants the right function for an application, and a language model that reads it to choose a function for someone. Both can start at Choose by use case, which goes from a need to a function, a backend and a program that shows it. The chapters after it teach one family of functions each, opening with two tables that compare everything in the family, what each function is and how to choose it; each section says what a function is for, shows a program of example/ that the build compiles and runs on every target with the output it prints, and lists the mistakes that cost security. Three chapters then follow an application from end to end: a peer-to-peer network, a cryptocurrency wallet, and the privacy of a login and a password manager. The reference that closes the page lists every name the headers declare, and llms.txt, beside this page, is the same guide as an index for language models (An index for language models).

Why hash

webcpp::hash is one entry point for hashing and key derivation in a C++ program, on every target webcpp has: native (Linux x86-64 and arm64, macOS arm64, Windows with MSVC), wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten. It is a wrapper: webcpp’s interface over code other projects wrote.

A hash function turns any amount of data into a short, fixed-size value, its digest, such that the same input always gives the same digest and different inputs, in practice, never do. A cryptographic hash adds that nobody can find two inputs with the same digest, or an input for a given digest, without an amount of work no computer will ever do. Everything else on this page is built from that property: a message authentication code is a hash that only the holder of a key can compute; a key derivation function turns one secret into several keys, or a password into a key; a password hash makes every guess of a stolen password database slow and costly. Each of them protects something an ordinary application holds: the integrity of a downloaded file, the authenticity of a request, the keys of an encrypted chat, the passwords of a login.

Every synchronous function reports failure as a value (boost::system::result), takes its data as std::span, and allocates nothing in webcpp’s own code (What each backend does with secrets and memory names what the C libraries allocate). <webcpp/hash/async.hpp> gives the slow ones and the ones WebCrypto has an asynchronous form, which completes through an event loop with a boost::system::error_code (Asynchronous calls).

The shape of a hash

A hash comes in two shapes. The types of algorithms.hpp, hmac.hpp, keccak.hpp and blake3.hpp have Boost.Hash2’s shape, the HashAlgorithm: construct it (with a key or a seed where it takes one), update it with bytes as often as the data arrives, and call result for the digest, a digest<N> of N bytes, or an integer for the non-cryptographic hashes and SipHash; the type is Hash2’s own, so every part of Hash2, hash_append and get_integral_result among them, takes it unchanged, and result can be called again. The families take a tag and a backend instead: digest_of hashes a message in one call, hasher takes it in pieces and gives exactly one result (a second finish is error::invalid_state), mac computes a tag in one call, and argon2 derives a key (One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher, A MAC in one call: mac). digest_of, mac, argon2 and every key derivation are functions that fill a caller’s std::span and return boost::system::result<void>; hasher is a type whose finish does the same.

The examples share one small header, example/hex.hpp, which writes bytes in hexadecimal and reads text and hexadecimal as bytes:

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

namespace example {

/** The bytes of `data`, two lowercase hexadecimal digits each. */
inline std::string hex(std::span<std::uint8_t const> data) {
    constexpr std::string_view digits = "0123456789abcdef";
    std::string out;
    out.reserve(2 * data.size());
    for (std::uint8_t const byte : data) {
        out += digits[byte >> 4U];
        out += digits[byte & 0x0fU];
    }
    return out;
}

/** The bytes of `text`, as they are: a password, a label, a message. */
inline std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes(std::string_view text) {
    // A char and a std::uint8_t share their object representation.
    return {reinterpret_cast<std::uint8_t const*>(text.data()), text.size()};
}

/** The bytes `text` writes in hexadecimal, two digits each. */
inline std::vector<std::uint8_t> from_hex(std::string_view text) {
    auto const digit = [](char c) {
        auto const u = static_cast<unsigned char>(c);
        return u <= '9' ? u - unsigned{'0'} : (u | 0x20U) - unsigned{'a'} + 10U;
    };
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> out(text.size() / 2);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < out.size(); ++i) {
        out[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>((digit(text[2 * i]) << 4U) | digit(text[(2 * i) + 1]));
    }
    return out;
}

}  // namespace example

What hash is not

hash is not a new implementation of a primitive: every permutation, compression function and hash is Boost.Hash2’s or a C library’s, and the two constructions webcpp writes over them are listed in The code webcpp writes, and what the C libraries do. It is not webcpp::crypto either: encryption, signatures, randomness and constant-time comparison stay there, and webcpp::crypto::equal is what compares a MAC. It holds primitives only: what a protocol defines on top of them (Bitcoin’s BIP39 seeds and hash160, Ethereum’s EIP-55 addresses, Nostr’s event ids and NIP-44’s keys) belongs to domain libraries, webcpp::bitcoin, webcpp::ethereum and webcpp::nostr, which build them from these functions. The chapters by use case show those steps as examples, each marked as what such a library builds, never as hash’s API.

Choose by use case

Find the need in the first column; the row names the function and its parameters, the backends that implement it with the line the program’s Jamfile adds, what to do about the backend, and the program of example/ that shows it. The section the function’s name links teaches it and its mistakes. The backend column is the capability table’s, doc/capabilities.json, and the table is generated from it and from doc/guide.json.

Three rules decide most cases that the table does not list.

  1. A password is never a key. Anything a person types and remembers is guessable: it goes through Argon2id (Argon2id) before it becomes a key, never through a digest, an HMAC or HKDF alone.

  2. A secret that is already random needs no slow function. A Diffie-Hellman result, a master key or 32 bytes from webcpp::crypto::random_device go through HKDF (HKDF), which is fast and separates each purpose by its info label.

  3. A standard names its function. Ethereum names Keccak-256, BIP39 names PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512, Nostr names SHA-256: use exactly what the format names, even where a newer function would be chosen for a new design.

Using webcpp::hash in your Jamfile

hash is header-only. A program names /webcpp/hash//hash, which adds hash’s include directory, Boost’s headers and webcpp’s configuration, and the C library of each part it uses; webcpp builds each C library from its pinned sources, for the program’s target:

The program uses Its Jamfile adds Targets

nothing more

keccak_256, or a tag on backends::xkcp (Keccak, SHA-3, SHAKE, SP 800-185, KMAC, KangarooTwelve, TurboSHAKE)

/third_party//xkcp

every target

blake3

/third_party//blake3

every target

argon2id, scrypt, blake2b_subkey, or HKDF, BLAKE2b, SipHash, SHA-2, SHA-3, SHAKE, TurboSHAKE, HMAC and argon2 on backends::sodium

/third_party//sodium

every target

HKDF, a digest or HMAC on backends::bearssl

/third_party//bearssl

every target

HKDF, PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2, KBKDF, the one-step KDF, the X9.63 KDF, a digest or a MAC on backends::openssl

/webcpp/hash//openssl

native, wasip2, wasip3

A program that hashes passwords with Argon2id and derives keys with HKDF on the default backend, backends::hash2, names, for example:

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/hash//hash /third_party//sodium ;

Each library’s target defines the macro WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_<NAME> that hash’s headers read, so linking a library is what makes its backend available; a program built without b2 defines the macro itself. libsodium and BearSSL are the same copies webcpp::crypto links, so a program of both libraries links each once. On Emscripten /third_party//sodium also links the program with -sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1, since Argon2id and scrypt allocate more than Emscripten’s fixed 16 MiB.

The library’s own target, as build.jam declares it:

alias hash : : : : <include>include <library>/boost//headers <library>/webcpp/config//config ;

When the build stops

A call that needs a library the program does not link, a backend that lacks the function, or two settings that contradict each other stops the build with a message that starts webcpp::hash: and says what to change. The messages, by what causes them:

Cause What to change

keccak_256, blake3, argon2id, scrypt, a backend, or a tag whose default is a backend, used without its library

The message is "…​ needs XKCP" (or BLAKE3’s C implementation, libsodium, BearSSL, OpenSSL) and gives the whole Jamfile line, as exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/hash//hash /third_party//xkcp ;: add that library.

/webcpp/hash//openssl on Emscripten

OpenSSL is not built for Emscripten: remove it; HKDF and PBKDF2 then run on backends::hash2.

pbkdf2 on backends::sodium or backends::bearssl

Neither library has PBKDF2: name backends::hash2 (every hmac) or backends::openssl (every hmac but hmac_ripemd_128).

hkdf_extract or hkdf_expand on backends::bearssl

BearSSL’s HKDF does both steps together: call hkdf, or name another backend.

HKDF over an hmac that backends::sodium or backends::bearssl does not have

The message lists the hmacs the backend has and the backends that have the one asked for.

hmac_ripemd_128 on backends::openssl

OpenSSL 3.5 has no RIPEMD-128: name backends::hash2.

kbkdf over an hmac backends::openssl does not have

No backend has it: use an hmac of hmac.hpp but hmac_ripemd_128.

sskdf or x963kdf over a digest its standard does not take

The message lists the digests the standard takes (SP 800-56C: SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3; ANSI X9.63: SHA-1, SHA-224 to SHA-512): name one.

argon2id or scrypt on another backend than backends::sodium or backends::openssl

Name one of them and add /third_party//sodium or /webcpp/hash//openssl.

blake2b_subkey on another backend than backends::sodium

Name backends::sodium and add /third_party//sodium.

A key derivation over a type that is not a Boost.Hash2 hmac of a digest

Pass an hmac, as hmac_sha2_256.

digest_of, hasher, mac or argon2 over a tag a backend does not have

The message names the backends that have it, as "digests::blake3 is not in this backend. Name one of: backends::blake3.": name one of them.

A tag with no default backend, called without a backend

The message is "…​ has no default backend. Name one of: …​": name one of the backends it lists as the second template argument.

digest_of, hasher, mac or argon2 over a type that is not a tag

Pass a tag of digests, macs, or kdfs::argon2id (argon2i, argon2d).

backends::webcrypto named in a synchronous function (hkdf, pbkdf2, digest_of, mac, …​)

WebCrypto is asynchronous: call async_hkdf (or async_pbkdf2, async_digest, async_hmac) with a completion token, or name a synchronous backend (Asynchronous calls).

backends::webcrypto named in an asynchronous function off Emscripten

It exists only on Emscripten: name a synchronous backend, or leave the default.

async_argon2id, async_argon2, async_scrypt or async_pbkdf2 (on a synchronous backend) in a build without threads

They run on another thread: natively remove WEBCPP_HASH_NO_THREADS; on Emscripten link with -pthread (b2’s threading=multi); on WASI call the synchronous function the message names.

async_digest, async_hmac or async_hkdf over an algorithm WebCrypto lacks

They take SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (and HMAC and HKDF over them): call the synchronous function the message names.

backends::webcrypto given the executor of a thread_pool (or of another context than an io_context)

WebCrypto’s promise settles in the JavaScript event loop, to which only the run of an io_context returns: pass the executor of the io_context run on the calling thread (WebCrypto in the browser). Behind any_io_executor the same mistake completes with invalid_parameters.

async_pbkdf2 on backends::webcrypto over an hmac WebCrypto lacks

WebCrypto’s PBKDF2 is over SHA-1 and SHA-2 alone: name a synchronous backend for the others.

Every message is tested: each is a test of test/messages/, which compiles a program that makes the mistake and checks the compiler prints the whole text, on every target where the mistake is possible; on Emscripten, where the messages of backends::webcrypto alone arise, the same program is a case of the superproject’s tools/test/hash_jamfiles_test.py.

Exceptions

hash raises no exception of its own: every operation that can fail reports it as a value, a boost::system::result, whether or not the program has exceptions. <webcpp/hash/config.hpp>, which every header of hash includes first, defines WEBCPP_HASH_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), and a program may define it for hash alone. Boost.Hash2’s types, on which every digest is built, do not throw either. Every test of hash runs twice, with exceptions and without.

Errors

Every operation of hash that can fail reports it with an error of the category webcpp.hash, as a boost::system::error_code. The values are fixed and never reused, so a program may store them. A guard runs before any work: a call it refuses leaves its output untouched; a backend that fails after it started zeroes the output, so that half a key is never used.

Value Name Raised when

1

invalid_output_size

The output is not of a size the function produces: empty, not a fixed-size digest’s size, or past the function’s limits (HKDF: past 255 times the digest; Argon2id: under 16 bytes; HMAC: under 10 bytes).

2

invalid_key_size

A key is not of a size the function takes: the pseudorandom key given to hkdf_expand is not of the hmac’s digest size; a MAC’s key is outside the MAC’s sizes (SipHash: 16 bytes; keyed BLAKE2b: 1 to 64 bytes; keyed BLAKE2s: 1 to 32 bytes; KMAC: at most SIZE_MAX / 8 bytes); the key option of the BLAKE2b digest is longer than 64 bytes; the master key of blake2b_subkey is not of 32 bytes; the secret or key of kbkdf, sskdf or x963kdf is empty.

3

invalid_salt_size

The salt is not of a size the function accepts (Argon2id: 16 bytes).

4

invalid_iterations

PBKDF2’s iteration count is zero, or more than the backend takes (backend_limits<Backend>::pbkdf2_iterations: 2^32 - 1 on backends::webcrypto).

5

invalid_parameters

A parameter is outside the function’s limits: a cost (Argon2id’s passes or memory, Argon2’s passes, lanes or memory, scrypt’s N, r and p); an option (BLAKE2b’s personalisation not of 16 bytes, TurboSHAKE’s domain byte outside 0x01 to 0x7F, ParallelHash’s block size of zero, the counter width of kbkdf other than 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits); the context of blake2b_subkey not of 8 bytes; an executor that backends::webcrypto cannot complete on.

6

input_too_long

An input is longer than the function or the backend accepts (HKDF’s info past 32,768 bytes; OpenSSL’s int lengths).

7

backend_failure

A backend failed where its contract says it does not.

8

unsupported_by_backend

A parameter the chosen backend does not take.

9

invalid_state

A hasher is used after its finish, once moved from, or after a backend failure spent it.

argon2id, argon2 and scrypt on every backend, kbkdf, sskdf and x963kdf, and every call on backends::openssl (a digest, a hasher, a MAC, a key derivation) also return errc::not_enough_memory of the generic category when the memory they need cannot be allocated: a program that handles the errors of hash checks that value too. A value that error does not define has the message "unknown webcpp.hash error".

Digests

A cryptographic digest is a fingerprint of data: a few dozen bytes that stand for a file, a message or a block of a chain, such that changing any bit of the data changes the fingerprint beyond recognition. It is what lets a file-sharing app check that the file it received is the one it asked for, a backup tool skip what it already stored, a wallet name a transaction, and a signature sign a short value instead of a whole document. A digest has no key: anybody can compute it, so it protects against accidents and against changes made where the attacker cannot also replace the digest. Where the attacker can, the answer is a MAC (Message authentication) or a signature.

Three properties make a hash cryptographic, each with its strength in bits: collision resistance (nobody finds two inputs with the same digest; at best half the digest’s bits, by the birthday bound), preimage resistance (nobody finds an input for a given digest) and second-preimage resistance (nobody finds another input with the digest of a given one). A digest of 256 bits gives 128-bit collision resistance, which no computer will reach; the "Security" column below gives each function’s.

SHA-2

SHA-2 is the family of digests NIST published in 2001 (FIPS 180-4 is its current text): SHA-224 and SHA-256 over 32-bit words, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 over 64-bit words. SHA-256 is the most widely deployed digest: TLS, Bitcoin, Git’s new object format, Nostr and every browser’s WebCrypto have it, and recent x86 and Arm processors compute it in hardware. Each is a Merkle-Damgård construction: the message, padded with its length, is cut into blocks, and a compression function folds each block into a state whose last value is the digest.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view const message = "abc";

    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 whole;
    whole.update(message.data(), message.size());
    auto const digest = whole.result();
    std::cout << "sha2_256(abc) " << example::hex(digest) << '\n';

    // The standard's own value: a program that prints something else has a bug, not a new hash.
    if (example::hex(digest) !=
        "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad") {
        return 1;
    }

    // Data that arrives in chunks (a socket, a file read in blocks) is hashed as it comes, without
    // collecting it first.
    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 pieces;
    pieces.update("a", 1);
    pieces.update("bc", 2);
    std::cout << "in two pieces " << (pieces.result() == digest ? "same" : "different") << '\n';
}
sha2_256(abc) ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
in two pieces same

Pitfalls.

  • Length extension. Whoever knows SHA-256(m) and the length of m can compute SHA-256(m || padding || x) for any x without knowing m. So the digest of a key followed by a message is not a MAC: an attacker appends to a signed request and computes its valid "tag". Use HMAC (HMAC), or a digest that resists it: SHA-384, SHA-512/256, SHA-3, BLAKE2 and BLAKE3.

  • A digest is not a password hash. SHA-256 runs at hundreds of megabytes per second; a stolen table of SHA-256 password digests is tested at billions of guesses per second on a graphics card. Passwords go through Argon2id (Argon2id).

  • A digest is compared as a public value. Comparing two digests with == is fine when both are public, a file’s expected digest for example; a tag that depends on a secret is compared with webcpp::crypto::equal (HMAC).

What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • bearssl: BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_hash.h states constant time for its GHASH implementations alone, not for br_md5_*, br_sha1_*, br_sha224_* to br_sha512_* or br_md5sha1_*.

  • hash2: Boost.Hash2 1.92: its headers (boost/hash2/) state no constant-time property.

  • openssl: OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_MD-*.pod, doc/man3/EVP_DigestInit.pod and providers/implementations/digests/ state no constant-time property.

  • sodium: libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

  • webcrypto: The Web Cryptography API (W3C Recommendation, 2017) states no constant-time property of digest, sign or deriveBits; each JavaScript runtime’s implementation decides, and webcpp reads none.

digests::md5_sha1 has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of digests::md5, digests::sha1, digests::sha2_224 and digests::sha2_384: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; bearssl, openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of digests::sha2_256 and digests::sha2_512: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; bearssl, openssl, sodium only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of digests::sha2_512_224 and digests::sha2_512_256: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

webcrypto serves the asynchronous family alone, on Emscripten, where the type of its asynchronous call names it (WebCrypto in the browser).

SHA-3 and SHAKE

SHA-3 is the standard NIST chose by an open competition and published in 2015 as FIPS 202: the Keccak team’s sponge. A sponge absorbs the message into a large state of 1,600 bits, a block at a time, mixing it with the Keccak-p permutation, then squeezes output from it. Its design shares nothing with SHA-2, which is why it exists: if a weakness were found in SHA-2, SHA-3 would not share it. It resists length extension by construction. SHA3-224 to SHA3-512 have fixed digest sizes; SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 are extendable-output functions (XOFs), which give as many bytes as the caller takes, and are what NIST’s post-quantum standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) use to expand seeds into matrices.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view const message = "abc";

    webcpp::hash::sha3_256 fixed;
    fixed.update(message.data(), message.size());
    std::cout << "sha3_256 " << example::hex(fixed.result()) << '\n';

    // SHAKE128 has no digest size: its output goes on as long as the caller asks. Hash2's
    // result() returns one whole block of 168 bytes, and each further call continues the stream.
    webcpp::hash::shake_128 xof;
    xof.update(message.data(), message.size());
    auto const first = xof.result();
    auto const second = xof.result();

    // The length is the caller's security choice. SHAKE128 has a 128-bit security strength, so
    // 32 bytes are as strong as it gets; keeping 16 bytes would give only 64 bits against
    // collisions. Take what the protocol needs and no less.
    constexpr std::size_t taken = 32;
    std::cout << "shake_128 first block " << example::hex({first.data(), taken}) << '\n';
    std::cout << "shake_128 second block " << example::hex({second.data(), taken}) << '\n';
}
sha3_256 3a985da74fe225b2045c172d6bd390bd855f086e3e9d525b46bfe24511431532
shake_128 first block 5881092dd818bf5cf8a3ddb793fbcba74097d5c526a6d35f97b83351940f2cc8
shake_128 second block 6aa01b3f5af057805f973ff8ecb8b226ac32ada6f01c1fcd4818cb006aa5b4cd

Pitfalls.

  • An XOF’s output length is the caller’s security choice. SHAKE128 gives at most 128-bit security however much is taken, and a short output gives less: 16 bytes give only 64-bit collision resistance. Take what the protocol names.

  • Hash2’s result() returns a whole block. Each call of result() on shake_128 returns the next 168 bytes of the stream (136 for shake_256), as Boost.Hash2 defines it; a program that wants bytes 32 to 63 takes them from the first block, not from a second call.

  • SHA3-256 is not Keccak-256. The padding differs (Keccak).

  • libsodium has SHA3-256, SHA3-512 and both SHAKEs too. digest_of and hasher reach them with backends::sodium named in the call (libsodium’s crypto_hash_sha3256, crypto_hash_sha3512 and crypto_xof_shake*, every output size), as they reach its SHA-256 and SHA-512 (One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher); the bytes are the same on every backend.

TurboSHAKE

TurboSHAKE128 and TurboSHAKE256 (RFC 9861, 2025, from the Keccak team) are SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 with half the rounds: the same sponge over the same 1,600-bit state, its permutation run 12 rounds instead of 24, which makes them roughly twice as fast with the same claimed security (128 and 256 bits; RFC 9861, sections 1 and 7). They are extendable-output functions, as SHAKE is, and take one parameter more: a domain separation byte D, from 0x01 to 0x7F (0x1F by default), absorbed after the message, so that each value is another function. A program that hashes several kinds of things gives each kind its own byte, and a value of one kind never stands for a value of another. TurboSHAKE is also the inner function of KangarooTwelve (KangarooTwelve (KT128 and KT256)). digest_of and hasher take the byte in digest_options<digests::turboshake_128> (or _256), on backends::xkcp, their default, XKCP’s own TurboSHAKE code, for which a program links /third_party//xkcp; or on backends::sodium, libsodium’s crypto_xof_turboshake128 and crypto_xof_turboshake256, named in the call. Both give the same bytes.

// TurboSHAKE128 of FF FF FF under two domain bytes: two unrelated functions.
auto const message = example::from_hex("ffffff");
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> first{};
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> second{};
if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::turboshake_128>(first, message, {.domain = 0x01}) ||
    !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::turboshake_128>(second, message, {.domain = 0x07})) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "turboshake_128 D=01 " << example::hex(first) << '\n';
std::cout << "turboshake_128 D=07 " << example::hex(second) << '\n';
turboshake_128 D=01 bf323f940494e88ee1c540fe660be8a0c93f43d15ec006998462fa994eed5dab
turboshake_128 D=07 b658576001cad9b1e5f399a9f77723bba05458042d68206f7252682dba3663ed

The same function on libsodium, named in the call:

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using webcpp::hash::backends::sodium;
    using webcpp::hash::digests::turboshake_128;

    // RFC 9861, section 5: TurboSHAKE128 of the empty message, D = 0x1F, 32 bytes.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> empty{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<turboshake_128, sodium>(empty, {})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "RFC 9861 " << example::hex(empty) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(empty) != "1e415f1c5983aff2169217277d17bb538cd945a397ddec541f1ce41af2c1b74c") {
        return 1;
    }

    // An extendable output: as many bytes as the caller takes, the shorter a prefix of the longer.
    auto const message = example::bytes("hello, world");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> id{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> longer{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<turboshake_128, sodium>(id, message) ||
        !hash::digest_of<turboshake_128, sodium>(longer, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "32 bytes " << example::hex(id) << '\n';
    std::cout << "64 bytes start alike: "
              << (std::ranges::equal(std::span(longer).first(32), id) ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // The domain byte (0x01 to 0x7F; 0x1F by default) makes another function from the same
    // permutation: an application gives each of its uses its own byte.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> other{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<turboshake_128, sodium>(other, message, {.domain = 0x0B})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "domain 0x0B " << example::hex(other) << '\n';

    // A hasher takes the domain byte when it starts.
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<turboshake_128, sodium>::make({.domain = 0x1F});
    if (!hashing || !hashing->update(example::bytes("hello, ")) ||
        !hashing->update(example::bytes("world"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> pieces{};
    if (!hashing->finish(pieces)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hasher " << (pieces == id ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // A domain byte outside RFC 9861's range is refused before any work.
    auto const refused = hash::digest_of<turboshake_128, sodium>(id, message, {.domain = 0x80});
    std::cout << "domain 0x80: " << refused.error().message() << '\n';
}
RFC 9861 1e415f1c5983aff2169217277d17bb538cd945a397ddec541f1ce41af2c1b74c
32 bytes 48bc83c7a80f5affa18f526c1e41b31bb83480b1c25f277cba6ce7b3f5f6fc34
64 bytes start alike: yes
domain 0x0B d9b578bfc741eca1dfee35ded1e8fa1af2c0aed72340083235e39bc5e288322c
hasher same
domain 0x80: a parameter is outside the function's limits

Pitfalls.

  • TurboSHAKE is not SHAKE. With 12 rounds instead of 24 it gives other bytes for the same message: a format that names SHAKE128 needs SHAKE128 (SHA-3 and SHAKE).

  • The domain byte is part of the function. Both sides of a protocol use the same byte for the same purpose; a byte outside 0x01 to 0x7F is refused (invalid_parameters) before any backend sees it, on every backend, although libsodium would accept it and XKCP would take any byte but 0, since RFC 9861 allows that range alone.

  • The output’s length is the caller’s security choice, as for SHAKE: 32 bytes of TurboSHAKE128 give 128-bit security, 16 bytes give only 64-bit collision resistance.

KangarooTwelve (KT128 and KT256)

KT128 and KT256 (RFC 9861) are KangarooTwelve, the Keccak team’s fast hash of large inputs: a tree over TurboSHAKE (TurboSHAKE) that cuts its input in chunks of 8,192 bytes, hashes each chunk on its own and hashes the results, so that an implementation can hash a large file on several cores or vector units, as ParallelHash does (cSHAKE, TupleHash and ParallelHash (SP 800-185)), but faster and with no block size to choose (RFC 9861, section 1). An input of up to 8,192 bytes is one TurboSHAKE call, so a short message costs little more. Both are extendable-output functions with the security of SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 (RFC 9861, section 7), and take a customisation string C, as cSHAKE does: an application gives each of its uses its own string, and the outputs are unrelated. They are tags of digest_of and hasher (One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher), on backends::xkcp, their default: XKCP’s own KangarooTwelve code, which computes the chunks one after another. A program links /third_party//xkcp.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

namespace hash = webcpp::hash;

int main() {
    // KT128 of RFC 9861's ptn(17), the bytes 00 to 10, with no customisation.
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> pattern(20000);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i != pattern.size(); ++i) {
        pattern[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i % 251);
    }
    std::span<std::uint8_t const> const file(pattern);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> digest{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::kt128>(digest, file.first(17))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "kt128 " << example::hex(digest) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(digest) !=
        "6bf75fa2239198db4772e36478f8e19b0f371205f6a9a93a273f51df37122888") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A file read in pieces, with the application's customisation string, which the hasher
    // reads at finish: `label` lives until then.
    auto const label = example::bytes("webcpp example");
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<hash::digests::kt128>::make({.customisation = label});
    if (!hashing) {
        return 1;
    }
    for (std::size_t at = 0; at < file.size(); at += 4096) {
        if (!hashing->update(file.subspan(at, std::min<std::size_t>(4096, file.size() - at)))) {
            return 1;
        }
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> pieces{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> once{};
    if (!hashing->finish(pieces) ||
        !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::kt128>(once, file, {.customisation = label})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "kt128 of the file " << example::hex(pieces) << '\n';
    std::cout << "pieces and one call agree: " << (pieces == once ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
    if (example::hex(pieces) !=
            "485b2905b93dacfa84cc6b94bef012cfd8aa9232aab119a0afae1073bd82c224" ||
        pieces != once) {
        return 1;
    }

    // TurboSHAKE128 of FF FF FF under two domain bytes: two unrelated functions.
    auto const message = example::from_hex("ffffff");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> first{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> second{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::turboshake_128>(first, message, {.domain = 0x01}) ||
        !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::turboshake_128>(second, message, {.domain = 0x07})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "turboshake_128 D=01 " << example::hex(first) << '\n';
    std::cout << "turboshake_128 D=07 " << example::hex(second) << '\n';
    return example::hex(first) ==
                       "bf323f940494e88ee1c540fe660be8a0c93f43d15ec006998462fa994eed5dab" &&
                   example::hex(second) ==
                       "b658576001cad9b1e5f399a9f77723bba05458042d68206f7252682dba3663ed"
               ? 0
               : 1;
}
kt128 6bf75fa2239198db4772e36478f8e19b0f371205f6a9a93a273f51df37122888
kt128 of the file 485b2905b93dacfa84cc6b94bef012cfd8aa9232aab119a0afae1073bd82c224
pieces and one call agree: yes
turboshake_128 D=01 bf323f940494e88ee1c540fe660be8a0c93f43d15ec006998462fa994eed5dab
turboshake_128 D=07 b658576001cad9b1e5f399a9f77723bba05458042d68206f7252682dba3663ed

Pitfalls.

  • A hasher reads C at finish. KangarooTwelve absorbs the customisation string after the message, and hasher keeps the span make took instead of copying it (no allocation): the bytes stay alive and unchanged until finish, or the digest is another one or the read is a dangling one. digest_of reads C during the call.

  • C is part of the function. KT128 with "app/v1" and KT128 with "app/v2" are unrelated; an empty C is the RFC’s default, and the 32-byte KT128 of a message with no C is what IANA’s "k12-256" names.

  • KT128 is not ParallelHash or BLAKE3. Each tree hash gives its own bytes: a format names one, and a file’s KT128 never matches another’s ParallelHash128.

  • The output’s length is the caller’s security choice, as for SHAKE: 32 bytes of KT128 give 128-bit security, 64 bytes of KT256 256-bit.

  • 32-bit XKCP counts chunks in a size_t. On wasm32 a message and C past a little under 32 TiB together would wrap XKCP’s count into a wrong digest; they are refused (input_too_long) before XKCP sees them.

What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • xkcp: XKCP at d20c8fc: README.markdown, lib/low/KeccakP-1600 and lib/high (KangarooTwelve, TurboSHAKE, Keccak/KeccakSponge) state no constant-time property.

The default of digests::kt128 and digests::kt256: xkcp on every target, whatever the program links (The default backend).

Keccak

Keccak-256 is Keccak as its authors submitted it to the SHA-3 competition, before NIST changed the padding for FIPS 202. Ethereum adopted it before the standard was final and kept it: an Ethereum address, a transaction id, a Solidity function selector and the state trie are all Keccak-256. hash’s keccak_256 runs XKCP’s Keccak-p[1600] permutation (the Keccak team’s own code) under a sponge written line for line as Boost.Hash2’s, so that it gives Hash2’s results for every sequence of calls (The code webcpp writes, and what the C libraries do, Upstream: Keccak in Boost.Hash2). A program links /third_party//xkcp.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/keccak.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view const empty;
    std::string_view const abc = "abc";

    webcpp::hash::keccak_256 keccak_of_empty;
    keccak_of_empty.update(empty.data(), empty.size());
    auto const empty_digest = example::hex(keccak_of_empty.result());
    std::cout << "keccak_256() " << empty_digest << '\n';

    webcpp::hash::keccak_256 keccak_of_abc;
    keccak_of_abc.update(abc.data(), abc.size());
    auto const abc_digest = example::hex(keccak_of_abc.result());
    std::cout << "keccak_256(abc) " << abc_digest << '\n';

    if (empty_digest != "c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470" ||
        abc_digest != "4e03657aea45a94fc7d47ba826c8d667c0d1e6e33a64a036ec44f58fa12d6c45") {
        return 1;
    }

    // Not the same function. Keccak-256 pads with the byte 0x01, SHA3-256 with 0x06, so a
    // program that calls one where a protocol names the other computes a digest nobody else
    // computes, and the error shows only as a signature or an address that does not match.
    webcpp::hash::sha3_256 sha3_of_empty;
    sha3_of_empty.update(empty.data(), empty.size());
    std::cout << "sha3_256() " << example::hex(sha3_of_empty.result()) << '\n';
}
keccak_256() c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470
keccak_256(abc) 4e03657aea45a94fc7d47ba826c8d667c0d1e6e33a64a036ec44f58fa12d6c45
sha3_256() a7ffc6f8bf1ed76651c14756a061d662f580ff4de43b49fa82d80a4b80f8434a

Pitfalls.

  • Keccak-256 is not SHA3-256. The two differ in one padding byte, 0x01 against 0x06, and give unrelated digests. A library that offers "SHA3" for Ethereum, or "Keccak" for a FIPS 202 format, computes a value nobody else computes, and the mistake shows only as an address or a signature that does not match. Use keccak_256 exactly where a format says Keccak-256.

Keccak-224, Keccak-384 and Keccak-512, the submission’s other sizes, are tags of digest_of and hasher (One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher): digests::keccak_224, digests::keccak_384 and digests::keccak_512, on backends::xkcp, which runs XKCP’s FIPS 202 code (Keccak_Hash) with Keccak’s padding, and on backends::openssl when the call names it. The same XKCP backend, named in the call, computes SHA3-224 to SHA3-512 and SHAKE128 and SHAKE256, any number of bytes of SHAKE’s stream; XKCP’s own test vectors (the ShortMsgKAT files), Boost.Hash2 and OpenSSL give the same values.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    auto const message = example::bytes("abc");

    // Keccak-512, the SHA-3 submission's padding: its default backend is XKCP.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> keccak{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::keccak_512>(keccak, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "keccak_512(abc) " << example::hex(keccak) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(keccak) !=
        "18587dc2ea106b9a1563e32b3312421ca164c7f1f07bc922a9c83d77cea3a1e5"
        "d0c69910739025372dc14ac9642629379540c17e2a65b19d77aa511a9d00bb96") {
        return 1;
    }

    // SHA3-256 on XKCP, named in the call: the same digest as on backends::hash2.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> sha3{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha3_256, hash::backends::xkcp>(sha3, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "sha3_256(abc) " << example::hex(sha3) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(sha3) != "3a985da74fe225b2045c172d6bd390bd855f086e3e9d525b46bfe24511431532") {
        return 1;
    }

    // SHAKE128 on XKCP: any length, here 200 bytes, past the first block of 168.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 200> shake{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::shake_128, hash::backends::xkcp>(shake, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "shake_128(abc), bytes 168 to 199: " << example::hex(std::span(shake).subspan(168))
              << '\n';
}
keccak_512(abc) 18587dc2ea106b9a1563e32b3312421ca164c7f1f07bc922a9c83d77cea3a1e5d0c69910739025372dc14ac9642629379540c17e2a65b19d77aa511a9d00bb96
sha3_256(abc) 3a985da74fe225b2045c172d6bd390bd855f086e3e9d525b46bfe24511431532
shake_128(abc), bytes 168 to 199: 6aa01b3f5af057805f973ff8ecb8b226ac32ada6f01c1fcd4818cb006aa5b4cd

Pitfalls.

  • The tag names the padding. digests::keccak_512 and digests::sha3_512 differ as keccak_256 and sha3_256 do: one byte of padding, unrelated digests. Keccak-224 to Keccak-512 are found in formats written before FIPS 202, rarely since; a new format takes SHA-3.

  • Keccak-224, Keccak-384 and Keccak-512 have no Hash2-form type here: their proposal to Boost.Hash2 is in Upstream: Keccak in Boost.Hash2, and until it lands they are reached through their tags alone.

cSHAKE, TupleHash and ParallelHash (SP 800-185)

NIST SP 800-185 builds three hashes on SHAKE, each for a job a plain digest does badly. cSHAKE is SHAKE with a customisation string: an application that hashes the same data for two purposes, an identifier and a checksum, gives each purpose its own string, and the two outputs are unrelated, so that a value computed for one can never be passed off as the other. TupleHash hashes a list of byte strings, a record’s fields, so that the bounds between them count: a signing app that hashes name then amount by plain concatenation gives ("ab", "c") and ("a", "bc") the same digest, and an attacker who controls one field can move bytes across the bound; TupleHash encodes each field’s length and cannot be fooled that way. ParallelHash cuts a long input in blocks of B bytes, hashes each block on its own and hashes the results, so that a large file can be hashed on several cores (backends::xkcp computes the blocks one after another); the block size is part of the function. All three come in a 128-bit and a 256-bit strength (SP 800-185, section 8.1) and give any number of bytes; TupleHash and ParallelHash have a fixed-length form, which encodes the output’s length so that their 32-byte and 64-byte digests are unrelated, and an XOF form, which does not. They are tags of digest_of and hasher (One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher), on backends::xkcp, their default: XKCP’s own SP 800-185 code. A program links /third_party//xkcp.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <initializer_list>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

namespace {

namespace hash = webcpp::hash;

// TupleHash128 of a tuple, one hasher update per element, into digest.
bool tuple_hash(std::initializer_list<std::span<std::uint8_t const>> elements,
                std::span<std::uint8_t> digest) {
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<hash::digests::tuplehash_128>::make();
    if (!hashing) {
        return false;
    }
    for (auto const element : elements) {
        if (!hashing->update(element)) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return hashing->finish(digest).has_value();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // cSHAKE128: SHAKE128 separated from every other use by the customisation string S.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> cshake{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::cshake_128>(
            cshake, example::from_hex("00010203"),
            {.customisation = example::bytes("Email Signature")})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "cshake_128 " << example::hex(cshake) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(cshake) !=
        "c1c36925b6409a04f1b504fcbca9d82b4017277cb5ed2b2065fc1d3814d5aaf5") {
        return 1;
    }

    // TupleHash128 of (00 01 02, 10 11 12 13 14 15): each update is one element.
    auto const first = example::from_hex("000102");
    auto const second = example::from_hex("101112131415");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tuple{};
    if (!tuple_hash({first, second}, tuple)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "tuplehash_128 " << example::hex(tuple) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(tuple) != "c5d8786c1afb9b82111ab34b65b2c0048fa64e6d48e263264ce1707d3ffc8ed1") {
        return 1;
    }

    // ParallelHash128 in blocks of 8 bytes, a block size the call states.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> parallel{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::parallelhash_128>(
            parallel, example::from_hex("000102030405060710111213141516172021222324252627"),
            {.block_size = 8})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "parallelhash_128 " << example::hex(parallel) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(parallel) !=
        "ba8dc1d1d979331d3f813603c67f72609ab5e44b94a0b8f9af46514454a2b4f5") {
        return 1;
    }

    // ("ab", "c") and ("a", "bc") concatenate to the same bytes and hash apart.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> ab_c{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> a_bc{};
    if (!tuple_hash({example::bytes("ab"), example::bytes("c")}, ab_c) ||
        !tuple_hash({example::bytes("a"), example::bytes("bc")}, a_bc)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "(ab, c) and (a, bc) differ: " << (ab_c != a_bc ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
    return ab_c != a_bc ? 0 : 1;
}
cshake_128 c1c36925b6409a04f1b504fcbca9d82b4017277cb5ed2b2065fc1d3814d5aaf5
tuplehash_128 c5d8786c1afb9b82111ab34b65b2c0048fa64e6d48e263264ce1707d3ffc8ed1
parallelhash_128 ba8dc1d1d979331d3f813603c67f72609ab5e44b94a0b8f9af46514454a2b4f5
(ab, c) and (a, bc) differ: yes

Pitfalls.

  • A TupleHash hasher takes one element per update. Feeding a field in two pieces makes two elements and another digest; digest_of hashes the tuple of one element, its input. The empty tuple (no update) and the tuple of one empty element differ.

  • The form is part of the digest. TupleHash128 and TupleHashXOF128 of the same input differ at every length, and so do the two forms of ParallelHash; the fixed-length form’s 32-byte digest is not the start of its 64-byte one. Choose the form the format names, with .xof.

  • ParallelHash’s block size has no default. SP 800-185 leaves B to the application, and a digest under another B is another digest: the call states it (.block_size; 0 is invalid_parameters). XKCP takes a power of two of at least 8 bytes and answers any other with unsupported_by_backend, NIST’s samples with B = 12 included; 8192 is common for large files.

  • The function name is NIST’s. cSHAKE’s function_name is reserved for functions NIST defines on it; an application separates its uses with customisation. With both empty, cSHAKE is SHAKE.

  • Lengths in bits. SP 800-185 counts every string in bits, which XKCP holds in a size_t: on wasm32 a customisation, a TupleHash element, a ParallelHash input (all its pieces together) or a fixed-length output past 512 MiB is refused (input_too_long, invalid_output_size) before XKCP sees it, rather than hashed into a wrong digest.

BLAKE2

BLAKE2 (RFC 7693) is a digest faster than MD5 in software and as strong as SHA-3, designed from BLAKE, a SHA-3 finalist. BLAKE2b works on 64-bit words and gives up to 64 bytes; BLAKE2s works on 32-bit words, for small machines, and gives up to 32 bytes. Both take a key, so a keyed BLAKE2 is a MAC without HMAC’s double pass (macs::blake2b_mac and macs::blake2s_mac, Keyed BLAKE2b on libsodium: macs::blake2b_mac). Argon2 is built on BLAKE2b, libsodium’s generic hash is BLAKE2b, and WireGuard uses BLAKE2s for its hash, its MAC and its HKDF.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view const message = "abc";

    webcpp::hash::blake2b_512 plain;
    plain.update(message.data(), message.size());
    auto const digest = example::hex(plain.result());
    std::cout << "blake2b_512(abc) " << digest << '\n';

    if (digest !=
        "ba80a53f981c4d0d6a2797b69f12f6e94c212f14685ac4b74b12bb6fdbffa2d1"
        "7d87c5392aab792dc252d5de4533cc9518d38aa8dbf1925ab92386edd4009923") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The key goes to the constructor, which is the RFC's key parameter: BLAKE2b mixes it in as
    // a first block of its own. Never prepend the key to the message yourself; that is a
    // different function, whose output matches no other implementation's keyed BLAKE2b.
    // Hash2's BLAKE2b has no salt or personalisation parameter: libsodium's crypto_generichash
    // has them, and a later increment of webcpp::hash.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    webcpp::hash::blake2b_512 keyed(key.data(), key.size());
    keyed.update(message.data(), message.size());
    std::cout << "keyed " << example::hex(keyed.result()) << '\n';
}
blake2b_512(abc) ba80a53f981c4d0d6a2797b69f12f6e94c212f14685ac4b74b12bb6fdbffa2d17d87c5392aab792dc252d5de4533cc9518d38aa8dbf1925ab92386edd4009923
keyed 9af0244b7da7fe29d90a89727e06a0c93977ce1ad7edcb76ac0b24142194ea00c77be4a1d3fededd31d5a593625a508e742fc90d708f8b48a5c246e4e8e42d94

Pitfalls.

  • The key goes to the constructor. blake2b_512(key, size) is RFC 7693’s key, up to 64 bytes (32 for BLAKE2s), mixed in as a block of its own; a key written into the message instead gives a different function, and a longer key gives a function no other BLAKE2 implementation computes, so keep keys at most 64 bytes (32 for BLAKE2s).

  • No salt, no personalisation, no variable length here. RFC 7693’s parameter block also carries a salt, a personalisation string (16 bytes for BLAKE2b, 8 for BLAKE2s) and the digest’s length; Boost.Hash2’s types fix them, so a digest cut to 32 bytes is not BLAKE2b-256, which encodes its length in its parameters. For BLAKE2b-256, or a salt or a personalisation, use digests::blake2b (BLAKE2b with a key, a salt, a personalisation and a length).

BLAKE2b with a key, a salt, a personalisation and a length

RFC 7693 defines BLAKE2b with four parameters besides the message, each written into the block that starts the hash, so that each choice is a different function: the output’s length (1 to 64 bytes), a key (up to 64 bytes, which makes it a MAC), a salt and a personalisation (16 bytes each). digest_of and hasher over the tag digests::blake2b take all four in digest_options<digests::blake2b>; the default backend, backends::sodium, is libsodium’s generic hash, crypto_generichash. A chat app that hashes message ids, attachment ids and contact keys personalises each kind, so that a value of one kind never stands for a value of another; a format such as Zcash’s transaction ids (ZIP 244) names BLAKE2b-256 with a personalisation of its own.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using webcpp::hash::digests::blake2b;
    auto const message = example::bytes("hello, world");

    // The personalisation is 16 bytes, one per kind of hash an application makes; the output's
    // size is an option, since BLAKE2b-256 is not BLAKE2b-512 cut short.
    auto const message_ids = example::bytes("chatapp.msg.v001");
    hash::digest_options<blake2b> const id_options{
        .personalisation = message_ids,
        .output_size = 32,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> id{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<blake2b>(id, message, id_options)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "message id " << example::hex(id) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(id) != "fa88bb46494debf0d96d9e2d15fb6ecc42d9ab6a1502e5900249db8274767960") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A hasher takes its options, the output's size among them, when it starts.
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<blake2b>::make(id_options);
    if (!hashing || !hashing->update(example::bytes("hello, ")) ||
        !hashing->update(example::bytes("world"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> pieces{};
    if (!hashing->finish(pieces)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hasher " << (pieces == id ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // Without the personalisation: another function, another value.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> plain{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<blake2b>(plain, message, {.output_size = 32})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "unpersonalised " << example::hex(plain) << '\n';

    // A key makes BLAKE2b a MAC: here a 16-byte tag under a 32-byte key.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> tag{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<blake2b>(tag, message, {.key = key, .output_size = 16})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "tag " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // A personalisation is 16 bytes or none: a shorter one is refused before any work.
    auto const refused = hash::digest_of<blake2b>(
        id, message, {.personalisation = example::bytes("chatapp"), .output_size = 32});
    std::cout << "7-byte personalisation: " << refused.error().message() << '\n';
}
message id fa88bb46494debf0d96d9e2d15fb6ecc42d9ab6a1502e5900249db8274767960
hasher same
unpersonalised 62fbf5098db33f5ee72f85b23b3751d39a2d8d8363f1c734bbb04e05ad2b3b58
tag d78577a3107d705547d17551fa69e742
7-byte personalisation: a parameter is outside the function's limits

Pitfalls.

  • The length is a parameter, not a cut. BLAKE2b-256 is not the first 32 bytes of BLAKE2b-512: the length goes in output_size, 64 by default, and the output given to digest_of or finish has exactly that size (invalid_output_size otherwise). A hasher takes it when it starts.

  • 16 bytes or nothing. A salt or a personalisation is 16 bytes or empty (invalid_salt_size, invalid_parameters); pad a shorter name yourself, the same way on every side, since the library does not guess a padding.

  • A key is a secret, the salt and personalisation are not. For a MAC, use a random key of 16 to 64 bytes from webcpp::crypto::random_device, compare tags with webcpp::crypto::equal, and prefer mac<macs::blake2b_mac> (Keyed BLAKE2b on libsodium: macs::blake2b_mac); a key of 0 bytes is the unkeyed hash.

  • backends::hash2 has BLAKE2b-512 alone. Named in the call, it answers unsupported_by_backend to a shorter output, a key, a salt or a personalisation, rather than ignore one.

BLAKE3

BLAKE3 (2020) is one function with four uses: a digest, a keyed hash (a MAC), a key derivation from a context string, and an extendable output. It splits the input into chunks of 1 KiB, hashes them independently and joins them in a binary tree, so it uses every SIMD lane of a processor and verifies a large file in parts; its rounds are fewer than BLAKE2’s. hash runs the official C implementation, with its SIMD code natively and the portable code on WebAssembly; a program links /third_party//blake3. In the measured data (Measured size and throughput), BLAKE3 is the fastest cryptographic digest natively on 1 MiB, and BLAKE2b is faster than BLAKE3 on wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/blake3.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    // The test vectors' input: bytes 0, 1, 2 ... 250, 0, 1 ... For one byte, a single zero.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 1> const input{0};

    // BLAKE3's plain hash. result() gives its 32 bytes.
    webcpp::hash::blake3 plain;
    plain.update(input.data(), input.size());
    auto const digest = example::hex(plain.result());
    std::cout << "hash " << digest << '\n';

    // The keyed hash is a MAC: the key is exactly 32 bytes, and the type says so.
    auto const key = example::bytes("whats the Elvish word for friend").first<32>();
    auto keyed = webcpp::hash::blake3::keyed(key);
    keyed.update(input.data(), input.size());
    auto const tag = example::hex(keyed.result());
    std::cout << "keyed_hash " << tag << '\n';

    // The key derivation takes a context, a string that names the purpose of the derived key:
    // the same secret under two contexts gives two unrelated keys, which is the point.
    auto derive =
        webcpp::hash::blake3::derive_key("BLAKE3 2019-12-27 16:29:52 test vectors context");
    derive.update(input.data(), input.size());
    auto const derived = example::hex(derive.result());
    std::cout << "derive_key " << derived << '\n';

    // Extendable output: any number of bytes from any position, without changing the hash. The
    // first 32 are the digest above.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> extended{};
    plain.squeeze(extended);
    auto const stream = example::hex(extended);
    std::cout << "extended " << stream << '\n';

    if (digest != "2d3adedff11b61f14c886e35afa036736dcd87a74d27b5c1510225d0f592e213" ||
        tag != "6d7878dfff2f485635d39013278ae14f1454b8c0a3a2d34bc1ab38228a80c95b" ||
        derived != "b3e2e340a117a499c6cf2398a19ee0d29cca2bb7404c73063382693bf66cb06c" ||
        stream !=
            "2d3adedff11b61f14c886e35afa036736dcd87a74d27b5c1510225d0f592e213"
            "c3a6cb8bf623e20cdb535f8d1a5ffb86342d9c0b64aca3bce1d31f60adfa137b") {
        return 1;
    }
}
hash 2d3adedff11b61f14c886e35afa036736dcd87a74d27b5c1510225d0f592e213
keyed_hash 6d7878dfff2f485635d39013278ae14f1454b8c0a3a2d34bc1ab38228a80c95b
derive_key b3e2e340a117a499c6cf2398a19ee0d29cca2bb7404c73063382693bf66cb06c
extended 2d3adedff11b61f14c886e35afa036736dcd87a74d27b5c1510225d0f592e213c3a6cb8bf623e20cdb535f8d1a5ffb86342d9c0b64aca3bce1d31f60adfa137b

The example’s inputs are those of BLAKE3’s official test vectors (test_vectors.json of its repository), and its outputs are theirs.

Pitfalls.

  • Three modes, three results. The plain hash, keyed(key_bytes) and derive_key(context_string) of the same input are unrelated; a verifier must use the mode the producer used.

  • A context names one purpose, forever. BLAKE3’s authors ask that a context string be hardcoded, globally unique and specific to one use, such as "example.com 2026-11-15 chat message keys": never a variable, never a secret. The key material goes through update.

  • The seeded constructor is a keyed hash. blake3(seed_value) and blake3(input_data, input_size) exist for Boost.Hash2’s HashAlgorithm form and key the hash with the seed; for a MAC, call keyed with a 32-byte key.

  • blake3 does not wipe itself. Like Hash2’s types, it holds the key in its state until it is destroyed; a program that needs the key gone writes over the object.

MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD: legacy

MD5 (1992) and SHA-1 (1995) are broken: collisions of MD5 are found in seconds; the first public collision of SHA-1, an identical-prefix one, SHAttered, came in 2017, and the first public chosen-prefix collision, two documents of the attacker’s choosing with one digest, SHA-1 is a Shambles, in 2019 (published 2020). RIPEMD-160 (1996) is not broken, but its 160 bits give 80-bit collision resistance, below what new designs accept, and RIPEMD-128 gives 64. hash keeps them because data and protocols use them: Git’s original object ids, old checksums, and Bitcoin’s hash160, RIPEMD-160 over SHA-256, in every legacy and SegWit v0 address (A Bitcoin address: hash160).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view const abc = "abc";

    webcpp::hash::ripemd_160 of_abc;
    of_abc.update(abc.data(), abc.size());
    auto const abc_digest = example::hex(of_abc.result());
    std::cout << "ripemd_160(abc) " << abc_digest << '\n';

    // Nothing to update: the digest of the empty message.
    webcpp::hash::ripemd_160 of_nothing;
    auto const empty_digest = example::hex(of_nothing.result());
    std::cout << "ripemd_160() " << empty_digest << '\n';

    if (abc_digest != "8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc" ||
        empty_digest != "9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31") {
        return 1;
    }
}
ripemd_160(abc) 8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc
ripemd_160() 9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31

Pitfalls. Never choose one of them for a new design: a signature over an MD5 or SHA-1 digest can be moved to a forged document. Read and check what already exists; write SHA-256, SHA-3 or BLAKE3. HMAC over MD5 or SHA-1 is not broken as a MAC, but it carries a broken name into audits; prefer hmac_sha2_256. MD5-SHA1, the 36 bytes TLS 1.0 and 1.1 sign (MD5 of the data, then SHA-1 of it; RFC 2246, section 4.7), is no stronger than SHA-1: digests::md5_sha1 has no default backend, and a program that must read old TLS data names backends::bearssl or backends::openssl (MD5-SHA1: TLS 1.0’s digest, on BearSSL or OpenSSL by name).

The default of digests::ripemd_160: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

MD5-SHA1: TLS 1.0’s digest, on BearSSL or OpenSSL by name

MD5-SHA1 is the 36-byte digest that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 sign and check: the MD5 of the data followed by the SHA-1 of the same data (RFC 2246, section 4.7). Its designers paired the two so that a break of one would not break the pair; Joux showed in 2004 that a collision of such a pair costs little more than a collision of its stronger half, and SLOTH (2016) turned the weakness into attacks on TLS. RFC 8996 deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in 2021. hash has it because a program that reads, replays or tests old TLS data needs the exact bytes: digests::md5_sha1 is in BearSSL (br_md5sha1_*) and OpenSSL (its "MD5-SHA1" digest) alone, so the call names backends::bearssl and the program links /third_party//bearssl, or names backends::openssl and links /webcpp/hash//openssl. No backend has an HMAC over it: no standard defines one. The same naming reaches BearSSL’s and OpenSSL’s other digests and MACs, which are never a default either.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using hash::backends::bearssl;
    auto const message = example::bytes("abc");

    // MD5-SHA1 has no default backend: the call names BearSSL.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 36> joined{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::md5_sha1, bearssl>(joined, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "md5_sha1 " << example::hex(joined) << '\n';

    // It is the two digests side by side, which the default backend computes one by one.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> md5{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 20> sha1{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::md5>(md5, message) ||
        !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha1>(sha1, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "md5 then sha1 " << example::hex(md5) << example::hex(sha1) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(joined) !=
        "900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A handshake's messages arrive one by one: a hasher on BearSSL takes them in pieces.
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<hash::digests::md5_sha1, bearssl>::make();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 36> pieces{};
    if (!hashing || !hashing->update(example::bytes("ab")) ||
        !hashing->update(example::bytes("c")) || !hashing->finish(pieces)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hasher " << (pieces == joined ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // Any digest BearSSL has is reached the same way, and gives the default backend's bytes.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> by_name{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> by_default{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha2_256, bearssl>(by_name, message) ||
        !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha2_256>(by_default, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "sha2_256 on bearssl " << (by_name == by_default ? "same" : "different") << '\n';
}
md5_sha1 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d
md5 then sha1 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d
hasher same
sha2_256 on bearssl same

Pitfalls.

  • Never for anything new. Its 288 bits suggest a strength it does not have: the pair is about as collision resistant as SHA-1, which is broken (MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD: legacy). Write SHA-256.

  • No default. digest_of<digests::md5_sha1> without a backend stops the build with a message that names backends::bearssl and backends::openssl; a program that names one without linking its library stops with a message that names the line to add.

  • The order is fixed. MD5’s 16 bytes come first, then SHA-1’s 20: SHA-1 followed by MD5 is another value, which a TLS 1.0 peer rejects.

SM3: China’s national digest

SM3 is the 256-bit digest of China’s commercial cryptography standards, published as GM/T 0004-2012 and as the national standard GB/T 32905-2016, and in ISO/IEC 10118-3 since 2018. Its design follows SHA-256’s (a Merkle-Damgard chain over 512-bit blocks), with its own message expansion and compression. A program needs it where a Chinese standard or regulator requires it: SM2 signatures hash with it, and RFC 8998 gives TLS 1.3 its ShangMi cipher suites. Elsewhere SHA-256 is the interoperable choice. hash has it on backends::openssl alone, OpenSSL 3.5.9’s default provider; it has no default backend, so the call names it and the program links /webcpp/hash//openssl (native, wasip2 and wasip3; OpenSSL is not built for Emscripten).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using hash::backends::openssl;
    auto const message = example::bytes("abc");

    // SM3 has no default backend: the call names OpenSSL, which the Jamfile links.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> once{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sm3, openssl>(once, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "sm3 " << example::hex(once) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(once) != "66c7f0f462eeedd9d1f2d46bdc10e4e24167c4875cf2f7a2297da02b8f4ba8e0") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The same digest in pieces: the hasher owns OpenSSL's context until it finishes.
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<hash::digests::sm3, openssl>::make();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> pieces{};
    if (!hashing || !hashing->update(example::bytes("a")) ||
        !hashing->update(example::bytes("bc")) || !hashing->finish(pieces)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hasher " << (pieces == once ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // Other digests of OpenSSL, each named: Keccak-256 (Ethereum's) and TLS 1.0's MD5-SHA1.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> keccak{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 36> md5_sha1{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::keccak_256, openssl>(keccak, message) ||
        !hash::digest_of<hash::digests::md5_sha1, openssl>(md5_sha1, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "keccak_256 " << example::hex(keccak) << '\n';
    std::cout << "md5_sha1 " << example::hex(md5_sha1) << '\n';
}
sm3 66c7f0f462eeedd9d1f2d46bdc10e4e24167c4875cf2f7a2297da02b8f4ba8e0
hasher same
keccak_256 4e03657aea45a94fc7d47ba826c8d667c0d1e6e33a64a036ec44f58fa12d6c45
md5_sha1 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d

Pitfalls.

  • No default. digest_of<digests::sm3> without a backend stops the build with a message that names backends::openssl; naming it without linking OpenSSL stops with a message that names the line to add.

  • OpenSSL allocates. A hasher on backends::openssl owns an EVP_MD_CTX that OpenSSL allocates with its own allocator when the hasher is made and frees when it finishes or is destroyed; digest_of allocates and frees one in each call (The code webcpp writes, and what the C libraries do).

One call, or pieces with one result: digest_of and hasher

The types above are Boost.Hash2’s form: an object fed with update whose result() can be called again, and which hash_append and the rest of Boost.Hash2 take. Two functions reach the same algorithms through a tag of webcpp::hash::digests, as digests::sha2_256, and a backend: digest_of hashes a message in one call, and hasher takes it in pieces, as a file read in blocks or a stream arrives, and gives exactly one result. The backend is the tag’s default, the first of backends::hash2, backends::xkcp, backends::blake3 and backends::sodium that has it, or the one the call names as its second template argument; the tables of each algorithm list them.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/digest.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    auto const message = example::bytes("abc");

    // One call: the tag names the algorithm, the default backend runs it (backends::hash2 here).
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> once{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha2_256>(once, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "digest_of " << example::hex(once) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(once) != "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad") {
        return 1;
    }

    // Data that arrives in pieces (a file read in blocks, a stream) goes through a hasher.
    auto hashing = hash::hasher<hash::digests::sha2_256>::make();
    if (!hashing || !hashing->update(example::bytes("a")) ||
        !hashing->update(example::bytes("bc"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> pieces{};
    if (!hashing->finish(pieces)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hasher " << (pieces == once ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // The result is final: a second finish is an error, not the hash of nothing more.
    auto const again = hashing->finish(pieces);
    std::cout << "second finish: " << again.error().message() << '\n';

    // A fixed-size digest takes its size alone: the output is refused before any work.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 20> too_short{};
    auto const refused = hash::digest_of<hash::digests::sha2_256>(too_short, message);
    std::cout << "20-byte output: " << refused.error().message() << '\n';

    // A backend named in the call: Boost.Hash2's SHAKE128, any size, the stream's first bytes.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> shake{};
    if (!hash::digest_of<hash::digests::shake_128, hash::backends::hash2>(shake, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "shake_128 " << example::hex(shake) << '\n';
}
digest_of ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
hasher same
second finish: the hasher was finished or moved from
20-byte output: the output is not of a size the function produces
shake_128 5881092dd818bf5cf8a3ddb793fbcba7

Pitfalls.

  • One result. A hasher gives its result once: a second finish, or an update after it, is error::invalid_state, not the hash of what came before; start another hasher for another message. A hasher is move-only, and wipes its state when it finishes, when it is destroyed and when it is moved from.

  • The output’s size is the digest’s. A fixed-size digest takes an output of exactly its size (invalid_output_size otherwise, the output untouched); an extendable-output function, SHAKE or BLAKE3, takes any size from 1 byte; BLAKE2b takes the size its options name (BLAKE2b with a key, a salt, a personalisation and a length).

  • A backend may have a tag in part. backends::hash2 has BLAKE2b with its 64-byte output and no option alone, and answers unsupported_by_backend to a shorter output or to an option; backends::openssl has BLAKE2b unkeyed, at every output size, with no key, salt or personalisation. A call that names a backend gets what that backend has, which its row of the tables says.

  • Some backends are reached only by name. backends::bearssl and backends::openssl are never a default. BearSSL’s MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2 and SHAKE (any output size) run only when the call names it, as digest_of<digests::sha2_256, backends::bearssl>, and the program links /third_party//bearssl; OpenSSL’s MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, SHAKE (any output size), Keccak, BLAKE2, RIPEMD-160, MD5-SHA1 and SM3 likewise, with /webcpp/hash//openssl. digests::md5_sha1 is in BearSSL and OpenSSL alone and has no default (MD5-SHA1: TLS 1.0’s digest, on BearSSL or OpenSSL by name). OpenSSL’s SHA-256/192 (SHA-256’s first 24 bytes) and its KMAC hash have no tag, and Whirlpool is in OpenSSL’s legacy provider, which webcpp does not load: the capability table says why.

  • A tag without its backend stops the build. A tag whose backend the program does not link stops with a message that names the line to add; a tag that the backend does not have stops with a message that names the backends that have it, or says that none has it (When the build stops).

Message authentication

A message authentication code (MAC) is a digest that only the holders of a secret key can compute. A server that signs its session cookies, an API that checks a request came from a client holding its key, a webhook receiver that checks the sender, and a chat protocol that rejects altered messages all do the same thing: the sender computes a tag from the key and the message, the receiver computes it again and accepts the message only if the two tags are equal. Without the key an attacker can neither forge a tag for a new message nor change a message and keep its tag. A MAC does not hide the message, and it does not prove to a third party who wrote it (both sides hold the key); that is a signature’s job, webcpp::crypto’s.

HMAC

HMAC (RFC 2104, 1997) turns any digest into a MAC: it hashes the key, padded to a block, with the message, then hashes that result again under the key padded another way. The double pass is what makes it safe over SHA-2 despite length extension, and HMAC remains secure even over hashes whose collision resistance is broken. HMAC-SHA-256 signs JSON Web Tokens (HS256), drives TLS 1.3’s key schedule through HKDF, and is in every browser’s WebCrypto. hash re-exports Boost.Hash2’s hmac<H> and one alias per Hash2 digest.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace {

webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256::result_type tag_of(std::span<std::uint8_t const> key,
                                                std::string_view message) {
    webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256 mac(key.data(), key.size());
    mac.update(message.data(), message.size());
    return mac.result();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    auto const key = example::bytes("Jefe");
    std::string_view const message = "what do ya want for nothing?";

    // The sender computes the tag and sends it along with the message.
    auto const tag = tag_of(key, message);
    std::cout << "hmac_sha2_256 " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(tag) != "5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The receiver computes the tag again from the message it got, and compares it with the one
    // it got. Never with ==: memcmp stops at the first different byte, so an attacker who
    // measures how long the answer takes learns how many leading bytes of a guess are right,
    // and guesses a valid tag one byte at a time. webcpp::crypto::equal reads every byte.
    bool const genuine = webcpp::crypto::equal(tag_of(key, message), tag);
    std::cout << "genuine: " << (genuine ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // One byte of the message changed in transit: the tags differ.
    bool const forged = webcpp::crypto::equal(tag_of(key, "what do ya want for nothing!"), tag);
    std::cout << "tampered: " << (forged ? "accepted" : "refused") << '\n';
    if (!genuine || forged) {
        return 1;
    }
}
hmac_sha2_256 5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843
genuine: yes
tampered: refused

Pitfalls.

  • Compare tags with webcpp::crypto::equal, never with ==. The digest’s operator== is memcmp, which returns at the first byte that differs; an attacker who sends guesses and times the answers learns how many leading bytes are right and builds a valid tag one byte at a time, in a few thousand tries per byte instead of 2256 in all. equal reads every byte whatever the data.

  • A key is random and as long as the digest. A 32-byte key from webcpp::crypto::random_device for HMAC-SHA-256; a password is not a key (Password hashing). A key longer than the hash’s block is hashed first, which gives it no more strength.

  • Authenticate everything the receiver acts on. A tag over the body alone lets an attacker change the headers, the recipient or the order of messages; put a version, the context and a counter or timestamp inside the authenticated bytes, with an unambiguous encoding (lengths, not separators).

  • Truncate only on purpose. A tag cut to 16 bytes still gives 128 bits against forgery; one cut to 4 bytes gives an attacker a one-in-four-billion chance per try, which a busy server can reach.
