What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • bearssl: BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_hmac.h states constant time for br_hmac_outCT alone; mac calls br_hmac_out.

  • hash2: Boost.Hash2 1.92: its headers (boost/hash2/) state no constant-time property.

  • openssl: OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man3/EVP_MAC.pod, doc/man7/EVP_MAC-HMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-KMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-BLAKE2.pod, EVP_MAC-Siphash.pod and providers/implementations/macs/ state no constant-time property.

  • sodium: libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

  • webcrypto: The Web Cryptography API (W3C Recommendation, 2017) states no constant-time property of digest, sign or deriveBits; each JavaScript runtime’s implementation decides, and webcpp reads none.

macs::hmac<digests::keccak_224> has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

macs::hmac<digests::keccak_256> has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

macs::hmac<digests::keccak_384> has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

macs::hmac<digests::keccak_512> has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

macs::hmac<digests::sm3> has no default backend: the call names one of its backends, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of macs::hmac<digests::md5>, macs::hmac<digests::sha1>, macs::hmac<digests::sha2_224> and macs::hmac<digests::sha2_384>: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; bearssl, openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of macs::hmac<digests::sha2_256> and macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512>: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; bearssl, openssl, sodium only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512_224>, macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512_256>, macs::hmac<digests::sha3_224>, macs::hmac<digests::sha3_256>, macs::hmac<digests::sha3_384>, macs::hmac<digests::sha3_512>, macs::hmac<digests::ripemd_160>, macs::hmac<digests::blake2b> and macs::hmac<digests::blake2s_256>: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

webcrypto serves the asynchronous family alone, on Emscripten, where the type of its asynchronous call names it (WebCrypto in the browser).

SipHash

SipHash (Aumasson and Bernstein, 2012) is a keyed hash made for one job: protecting hash tables whose keys come from someone else. A hash table puts each key in a bucket chosen by its hash; with an unkeyed hash, FNV or MurmurHash or xxHash, anyone can compute in advance thousands of keys that fall in one bucket, send them as the names in a form, the fields of a JSON document or the ids of peers, and turn every lookup into a scan of a long list: a denial of service called hash flooding. With SipHash keyed by a secret random key per process, the attacker cannot predict the buckets. Python’s dictionaries, Rust’s HashMap and the Linux kernel use it for that reason. siphash_64 is SipHash-2-4 with a 16-byte key and a 64-bit result; siphash_32 is HalfSipHash-2-4, the 32-bit variant for small machines, with an 8-byte key and a 32-bit result.

This section adapts the guidance of libsodium’s documentation on short-input hashing (hashing/short-input_hashing.md of libsodium-doc, ISC licence, kept in NOTICE.md), in hash’s own terms.

#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_set>

namespace {

// A hasher for a hash table of ids that arrive from the network, keyed with a secret.
struct peer_hasher {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> key;

    std::size_t operator()(std::string const& id) const {
        webcpp::hash::siphash_64 h(key.data(), key.size());
        h.update(id.data(), id.size());
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(h.result());
    }
};

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> key{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 15> message{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < message.size(); ++i) {
        message[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }

    // The 64-bit hash takes a 16-byte key.
    webcpp::hash::siphash_64 wide(key.data(), key.size());
    wide.update(message.data(), message.size());
    std::uint64_t const wide_value = wide.result();

    // The 32-bit hash takes an 8-byte key: HalfSipHash, for the targets where 32-bit words are
    // the natural size.
    webcpp::hash::siphash_32 narrow(key.data(), 8);
    narrow.update(message.data(), message.size());
    std::uint32_t const narrow_value = narrow.result();

    std::cout << std::hex << std::setfill('0');
    std::cout << "siphash_64 " << std::setw(16) << wide_value << '\n';
    std::cout << "siphash_32 " << std::setw(8) << narrow_value << '\n';
    std::cout << std::dec;
    if (wide_value != 0xa129ca6149be45e5ULL || narrow_value != 0x972bfe74U) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The use. A table keyed by an unkeyed hash (FNV, xxHash) lets an attacker who chooses the
    // keys choose keys that all collide, and the table degrades to a list: hash flooding. A
    // random key, secret and different in every process, takes that choice away from the attacker.
    peer_hasher hasher{};
    auto const filled = webcpp::crypto::random_device{}.fill(hasher.key);
    if (!filled) {
        std::cerr << filled.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::unordered_set<std::string, peer_hasher> peers(8, hasher);
    peers.insert("peer-a");
    peers.insert("peer-b");
    peers.insert("peer-c");
    std::cout << "peers " << peers.size() << '\n';
}
siphash_64 a129ca6149be45e5
siphash_32 972bfe74
peers 3

Pitfalls.

  • The key is the protection. A key that an attacker can read or guess (a constant, a seed from the time) gives no protection at all; draw it from webcpp::crypto::random_device when the process starts, and keep it secret.

  • Not a digest and not a MAC for messages. 64 bits are too few to resist collisions found on purpose, and 32 bits far too few: SipHash protects the shape of a table, not the integrity of data. Use HMAC (HMAC) for messages.

  • Use every bit when choosing a bucket. A table that keeps only the low bits of the hash, or reduces it by a power of two, throws away part of what the key protects; a prime number of buckets, or a multiply-and-shift reduction, keeps them.

KMAC

KMAC (NIST SP 800-185, section 4) is a MAC built on cSHAKE, the SHA-3 family’s own: where HMAC wraps a hash twice around the key to protect it from the hash’s structure, KMAC needs no wrapping, since SHA-3’s sponge already keeps its state hidden. It takes a key, the message and a customisation string that separates one application’s tags from another’s under the same key, and gives a tag of any length; NIST’s key derivation (SP 800-56C) uses it too. Like TupleHash, it has a fixed-length form, which encodes the tag’s length, and an XOF form, KMACXOF, which does not. macs::kmac_128 and macs::kmac_256 are tags of mac (A MAC in one call: mac), on backends::xkcp, their default; a program links /third_party//xkcp. backends::openssl has them too, named in the call, within OpenSSL’s narrower limits (The MACs of OpenSSL: KMAC, keyed BLAKE2, SipHash and HMAC).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using webcpp::hash::macs::kmac_128;

    auto const key =
        example::from_hex("404142434445464748494a4b4c4d4e4f505152535455565758595a5b5c5d5e5f");
    auto const message = example::from_hex("00010203");
    auto const application = example::bytes("My Tagged Application");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    if (!hash::mac<kmac_128>(tag, key, message, {.customisation = application})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "kmac_128 " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(tag) != "3b1fba963cd8b0b59e8c1a6d71888b7143651af8ba0a7070c0979e2811324aa5") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The receiver computes the tag again and compares it in constant time, never with ==.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> expected{};
    bool const genuine =
        hash::mac<kmac_128>(expected, key, message, {.customisation = application}).has_value() &&
        webcpp::crypto::equal(expected, tag);
    std::cout << "genuine: " << (genuine ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // KMACXOF128: the same inputs, another tag.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> xof{};
    if (!hash::mac<kmac_128>(xof, key, message, {.customisation = application, .xof = true})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "kmacxof_128 " << example::hex(xof) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(xof) != "31a44527b4ed9f5c6101d11de6d26f0620aa5c341def41299657fe9df1a3b16c") {
        return 1;
    }
    return genuine ? 0 : 1;
}
kmac_128 3b1fba963cd8b0b59e8c1a6d71888b7143651af8ba0a7070c0979e2811324aa5
genuine: yes
kmacxof_128 31a44527b4ed9f5c6101d11de6d26f0620aa5c341def41299657fe9df1a3b16c

Pitfalls.

  • Compare with webcpp::crypto::equal. As for every tag (HMAC).

  • The key sets the strength. SP 800-185 (section 8.4.1) forbids a key shorter than the security the application needs: 16 bytes for KMAC128, 32 for KMAC256. mac takes any key, the empty one included, as the standard defines it; choose its size.

  • At least 4 bytes of tag. SP 800-185 (section 8.4.2) forbids a tag of fewer than 32 bits and asks for a careful analysis below 64; mac refuses a tag under 4 bytes with invalid_output_size. Prefer 16 bytes or more.

  • The form is part of the tag. KMAC128 and KMACXOF128 of the same inputs differ, and a fixed-length tag of 16 bytes is not the start of one of 32: the receiver uses the sender’s form and length.

A MAC in one call: mac

mac computes the tag of a message under a key in one call, through a tag of webcpp::hash::macs, as macs::hmac<digests::sha2_256>, HMAC over the digest digests::sha2_256, and a backend: the tag’s default, or the one the call names. Its guards are the same on every backend: an HMAC tag is 10 bytes up to the digest’s size, a shorter one being the digest cut (RFC 2104, section 5); a key of a size the MAC does not take is invalid_key_size. The Hash2 aliases of HMAC stay the way to feed a message in pieces.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using hmac_sha256 = hash::macs::hmac<hash::digests::sha2_256>;

    auto const key = example::bytes("Jefe");
    auto const message = example::bytes("what do ya want for nothing?");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    if (!hash::mac<hmac_sha256>(tag, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "mac " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(tag) != "5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The receiver computes the tag again and compares it in constant time, never with ==.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> expected{};
    bool const genuine = hash::mac<hmac_sha256>(expected, key, message).has_value() &&
                         webcpp::crypto::equal(expected, tag);
    std::cout << "genuine: " << (genuine ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // A tag cut to 16 bytes is the digest's first 16 (RFC 2104, section 5); shorter than 10 is
    // refused.
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> const key_5(20, 0x0c);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> cut{};
    if (!hash::mac<hmac_sha256>(cut, key_5, example::bytes("Test With Truncation"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "cut to 16 " << example::hex(cut) << '\n';
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> too_short{};
    std::cout << "8-byte tag: " << hash::mac<hmac_sha256>(too_short, key, message).error().message()
              << '\n';
    return genuine ? 0 : 1;
}
mac 5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843
genuine: yes
cut to 16 a3b6167473100ee06e0c796c2955552b
8-byte tag: the output is not of a size the function produces

Pitfalls.

  • Compare with webcpp::crypto::equal. As for every tag (HMAC).

  • A cut tag is a weaker tag. Ten bytes, 80 bits, is the shortest mac gives; keep the whole digest unless a protocol fixes a shorter tag.

  • The tag’s name is the digest’s. macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512> cut to 32 bytes is not HMAC over SHA-512/256 (macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512_256>): the two give different tags.

  • BearSSL’s HMAC is reached by name. backends::bearssl has HMAC over MD5, SHA-1 and the four SHA-2s it has, any key and any tag mac accepts, but is never a default: name it, as mac<macs::hmac<digests::sha2_256>, backends::bearssl>, and link /third_party//bearssl.

  • Keyed BLAKE2s on backends::hash2 is 32 bytes. macs::blake2s_mac takes a tag of 1 to 32 bytes, but BLAKE2s’s output size is a parameter of the hash, not a cut: backends::hash2 (Boost.Hash2’s keyed blake2s_256) answers unsupported_by_backend to a shorter tag. macs::siphash_2_4 on it is SipHash-2-4 whole: a 16-byte key and an 8-byte tag.

SipHash on libsodium: macs::siphash_2_4x

mac computes SipHash through two tags: macs::siphash_2_4, SipHash-2-4 with its 8-byte result, on backends::hash2 (Boost.Hash2’s siphash_64, the default) or on backends::sodium (libsodium’s crypto_shorthash_siphash24), which give the same bytes; and macs::siphash_2_4x, the same rounds with a 16-byte result (the SipHash reference implementation’s 128-bit output, libsodium’s crypto_shorthash_siphashx24), on backends::sodium alone, its default. Both take a 16-byte key. The 16-byte result makes collisions between honest keys rare enough for a table or a filter of billions of entries, or for a short identifier keyed against flooding, where 64 bits would collide; it is still a hash for tables, not a MAC for messages (SipHash).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    namespace macs = hash::macs;

    auto const key = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f");
    auto const message = example::bytes("user:alice");

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> on_sodium{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> on_hash2{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::siphash_2_4, hash::backends::sodium>(on_sodium, key, message) ||
        !hash::mac<macs::siphash_2_4>(on_hash2, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "siphash_2_4 " << example::hex(on_sodium) << '\n';
    std::cout << "the same on hash2: " << (on_sodium == on_hash2 ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // SipHash-2-4x: 16 bytes, another value than SipHash-2-4's, not two of its tags side by side.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> wide{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::siphash_2_4x>(wide, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "siphash_2_4x " << example::hex(wide) << '\n';

    // The key is 16 bytes, always.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> const short_key{};
    std::cout << "8-byte key: "
              << hash::mac<macs::siphash_2_4x>(wide, short_key, message).error().message() << '\n';
    return on_sodium == on_hash2 ? 0 : 1;
}
siphash_2_4 9737f8b03db06d4b
the same on hash2: yes
siphash_2_4x e0f98248d7904e01892c15a501078e28
8-byte key: the key is not of a size the function accepts

Pitfalls.

  • The pitfalls of SipHash hold: a random key per process, and not a MAC for messages: use HMAC there.

  • SipHash-2-4x is not two SipHash-2-4 tags. Its 16 bytes are another function’s output, and its first 8 bytes are not SipHash-2-4’s tag: a program that must agree with another names the same tag.

  • The tag is written little-endian. mac writes SipHash-2-4’s 64-bit result as 8 bytes, least significant first, as the reference implementation and libsodium do; the result() of siphash_64 is the number itself.

HMAC on libsodium

mac computes HMAC over SHA-256 and SHA-512 on backends::sodium too, with libsodium’s crypto_auth_hmacsha256 and crypto_auth_hmacsha512 functions, named in the call: the same tags as the default, backends::hash2, for a program that already links libsodium or that wants its implementation. libsodium names a third HMAC, crypto_auth_hmacsha512256, "HMAC-SHA-512-256": it is HMAC-SHA-512 cut to 32 bytes, which mac over digests::sha2_512 gives with a 32-byte output, and not HMAC over SHA-512/256 (macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512_256>), a different function that libsodium does not have.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    namespace digests = webcpp::hash::digests;
    using webcpp::hash::backends::sodium;
    using webcpp::hash::macs::hmac;

    // A 32-byte key, as webcpp::crypto::random_device gives it (fixed here, for the output).
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    auto const message = example::bytes("hello, world");

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    if (!hash::mac<hmac<digests::sha2_256>, sodium>(tag, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "HMAC-SHA-256 " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // The receiver computes the tag again and compares it in constant time.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> again{};
    bool const genuine = hash::mac<hmac<digests::sha2_256>, sodium>(again, key, message) &&
                         webcpp::crypto::equal(again, tag);
    std::cout << "genuine: " << (genuine ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // libsodium's crypto_auth_hmacsha512256 is HMAC-SHA-512 cut to 32 bytes: the same tag, with a
    // 32-byte output.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> cut{};
    if (!hash::mac<hmac<digests::sha2_512>, sodium>(cut, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "HMAC-SHA-512 cut to 32 " << example::hex(cut) << '\n';

    // HMAC over SHA-512/256 is another function, which libsodium does not have.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> over_512_256{};
    if (!hash::mac<hmac<digests::sha2_512_256>>(over_512_256, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "HMAC over SHA-512/256 " << example::hex(over_512_256) << '\n';
    return genuine ? 0 : 1;
}
HMAC-SHA-256 fe751971276e8bc03a398380b60d4cbfcde5da9a4a834f610fd82bff4daa3257
genuine: yes
HMAC-SHA-512 cut to 32 d8898906eb374195bd7acd21aad5017aedd46d80e5355399c954800c3c5f622c
HMAC over SHA-512/256 1d28354e16fb041be89d848b9f14c1c5188c332d68d95fc0004ed91af7f75619

Pitfalls.

  • The pitfalls of HMAC hold: compare tags with webcpp::crypto::equal, and use a random key, not a password.

  • "HMAC-SHA-512-256" has two meanings. A program that must agree with libsodium’s crypto_auth_hmacsha512256 names macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512> and a 32-byte output; one that follows a standard naming HMAC over SHA-512/256 names macs::hmac<digests::sha2_512_256>. The two give different tags.

  • A key of any size. libsodium’s one-call functions take a 32-byte key alone; mac on backends::sodium takes a key of any size, hashed first when it is longer than the block, as RFC 2104 says and as every other backend does.

Keyed BLAKE2b on libsodium: macs::blake2b_mac

Keyed BLAKE2b (RFC 7693, section 2.5) is a MAC by itself: the key goes into the hash’s first block, so it needs neither HMAC’s second pass nor its construction. mac<macs::blake2b_mac> computes it on backends::sodium, its default (libsodium’s keyed crypto_generichash_blake2b), with a key of 1 to 64 bytes and a tag of 1 to 64 bytes; a program links /third_party//sodium, on every target. backends::openssl gives the same tags, named in the call (The MACs of OpenSSL: KMAC, keyed BLAKE2, SipHash and HMAC).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using webcpp::hash::macs::blake2b_mac;

    // A 32-byte key, as webcpp::crypto::random_device gives it (fixed here, for the output).
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    auto const message = example::bytes("order:42,amount:10.00");

    // The default backend of macs::blake2b_mac is backends::sodium: link /third_party//sodium.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    if (!hash::mac<blake2b_mac>(tag, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "BLAKE2b-256 keyed " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // The receiver computes the tag again and compares it in constant time.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> again{};
    bool const genuine =
        hash::mac<blake2b_mac>(again, key, message) && webcpp::crypto::equal(again, tag);
    std::cout << "genuine: " << (genuine ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // The tag's size is a parameter of the hash: a 16-byte tag is not the 32-byte one cut.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> short_tag{};
    if (!hash::mac<blake2b_mac>(short_tag, key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "BLAKE2b-128 keyed " << example::hex(short_tag) << '\n';

    // An empty key is the unkeyed hash, a digest (digests::blake2b), not a MAC.
    std::cout
        << "empty key: "
        << hash::mac<blake2b_mac>(tag, std::span<std::uint8_t const>{}, message).error().message()
        << '\n';
    return genuine ? 0 : 1;
}
BLAKE2b-256 keyed f857e744317936fbea0cf4b2354ca9fb0c48cf6dc66b48b07facec64d943c712
genuine: yes
BLAKE2b-128 keyed dcb107ed916a53063ae35186bfb06720
empty key: the key is not of a size the function accepts

Pitfalls.

  • Compare with webcpp::crypto::equal. As for every tag (HMAC).

  • The length is a parameter, not a cut. The tag’s size goes into the hash: a 16-byte tag is not the first 16 bytes of a 32-byte one, and the receiver uses the sender’s size.

  • Draw a key of 32 random bytes. mac takes every size RFC 7693 gives, from 1 byte (libsodium’s 16-byte minimums are advice its functions do not check), but the key sets the strength: draw 32 bytes from webcpp::crypto::random_device. An empty key is invalid_key_size: unkeyed BLAKE2b is a digest (BLAKE2b with a key, a salt, a personalisation and a length).

  • libsodium’s state is wiped. mac keeps libsodium’s BLAKE2b state, which holds the key, in its own frame and wipes it before it returns.

What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • hash2: Boost.Hash2 1.92: its headers (boost/hash2/) state no constant-time property.

  • openssl: OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man3/EVP_MAC.pod, doc/man7/EVP_MAC-HMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-KMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-BLAKE2.pod, EVP_MAC-Siphash.pod and providers/implementations/macs/ state no constant-time property.

  • sodium: libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

The default of macs::blake2b_mac: sodium on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The default of macs::blake2s_mac: hash2 on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

The MACs of OpenSSL: KMAC, keyed BLAKE2, SipHash and HMAC

backends::openssl computes every tag of webcpp::hash::macs through OpenSSL 3.5.9’s EVP_MAC, on native, wasip2 and wasip3. It is never a default (design D34): a call names it. Its tags are HMAC over every digest of a fixed size it has but MD5-SHA1, over which no standard defines an HMAC, macs::hmac<digests::keccak_256> and macs::hmac<digests::sm3> among them, which no other backend has; KMAC128 and KMAC256 (NIST SP 800-185, section 4), macs::kmac_128 and macs::kmac_256, in their fixed-length and XOF forms, with a customisation string; keyed BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s (RFC 7693), macs::blake2b_mac and macs::blake2s_mac, at every tag size; and SipHash-2-4 with an 8-byte or a 16-byte tag. KMAC encodes the tag’s length in its fixed-length form, so that two tags of different sizes are unrelated; its XOF form (.xof = true) encodes none, and a shorter tag is the start of a longer.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/mac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    namespace macs = hash::macs;
    using hash::backends::openssl;

    // KMAC128 with a customisation string: NIST's sample #2.
    auto const key =
        example::from_hex("404142434445464748494a4b4c4d4e4f505152535455565758595a5b5c5d5e5f");
    auto const data = example::from_hex("00010203");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> kmac{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::kmac_128, openssl>(
            kmac, key, data, {.customisation = example::bytes("My Tagged Application")})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "kmac_128 " << example::hex(kmac) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(kmac) != "3b1fba963cd8b0b59e8c1a6d71888b7143651af8ba0a7070c0979e2811324aa5") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The XOF form encodes no length: its 16 bytes are the start of its 32.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> long_xof{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> short_xof{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::kmac_128, openssl>(long_xof, key, data, {.xof = true}) ||
        !hash::mac<macs::kmac_128, openssl>(short_xof, key, data, {.xof = true})) {
        return 1;
    }
    bool const prefix = std::equal(short_xof.begin(), short_xof.end(), long_xof.begin());
    std::cout << "kmacxof_128 16 bytes are the start of 32: " << (prefix ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';

    // HMAC over SM3, which has no default backend.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> hmac_sm3{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::hmac<hash::digests::sm3>, openssl>(
            hmac_sm3, example::bytes("Jefe"), example::bytes("what do ya want for nothing?"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "hmac sm3 " << example::hex(hmac_sm3) << '\n';

    // Keyed BLAKE2b of 32 bytes, its size a parameter of the hash, not a cut.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> blake2b_key{};
    std::iota(blake2b_key.begin(), blake2b_key.end(), std::uint8_t{0});
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> blake2b{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::blake2b_mac, openssl>(blake2b, blake2b_key, example::bytes("abc"))) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "blake2b_mac " << example::hex(blake2b) << '\n';

    // SipHash-2-4 with a 16-byte tag.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> siphash_key{};
    std::iota(siphash_key.begin(), siphash_key.end(), std::uint8_t{0});
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> siphash{};
    if (!hash::mac<macs::siphash_2_4x, openssl>(siphash, siphash_key, {})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "siphash_2_4x " << example::hex(siphash) << '\n';

    // OpenSSL's KMAC takes a key of 4 to 512 bytes, narrower than SP 800-185.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 3> const short_key{1, 2, 3};
    std::cout << "3-byte KMAC key: "
              << hash::mac<macs::kmac_128, openssl>(kmac, short_key, data).error().message()
              << '\n';
    return prefix ? 0 : 1;
}

kmacxof_128 16 bytes are the start of 32: yes
hmac sm3 2e87f1d16862e6d964b50a5200bf2b10b764faa9680a296a2405f24bec39f882
blake2b_mac d63a32d3e44738d7907f964316c241adaba0abfeabc32349677578a15a203f7f
siphash_2_4x a3817f04ba25a8e66df67214c7550293
3-byte KMAC key: the backend does not take this parameter; name a backend that does

Pitfalls.

  • OpenSSL’s KMAC is narrower than SP 800-185. It takes a key of 4 to 512 bytes, a customisation of at most 512 bytes and a tag of at most 2,097,151 bytes, in either form; mac answers any other unsupported_by_backend before OpenSSL is called. A tag under 4 bytes is invalid_output_size on every backend: SP 800-185, section 8.4.2, forbids a MAC of fewer than 32 bits.

  • The customisation separates applications, the key keeps the secret. Two programs that share a key and differ in their customisation string get unrelated tags; the string itself is not secret.

  • Keyed BLAKE2 takes a key of at least one byte. An empty key is invalid_key_size (RFC 7693’s keyed mode has a key of 1 to 64 bytes, 1 to 32 for BLAKE2s); unkeyed BLAKE2 is a digest (BLAKE2b with a key, a salt, a personalisation and a length).

  • Each call allocates through OpenSSL. The MAC and its context are fetched, made and freed in the call (EVP_MAC_CTX_new), as for every function of this backend (Allocation); OpenSSL documents that it frees them, not that it clears them. Its HMAC, KMAC and BLAKE2 MACs clear their copy of the key when freed (the BLAKE2 MACs’ first block, which holds the key too, only once the tag is computed, not when a call fails before); its SipHash frees its keyed state without clearing it.

  • An HMAC key is at most INT_MAX bytes on OpenSSL, which takes its length as an int; a longer one is unsupported_by_backend.

The backends of each tag are in the tables of KMAC, Keyed BLAKE2b on libsodium: macs::blake2b_mac, SipHash and HMAC.

Key derivation

A key derivation function (KDF) turns secret material that is not fit to be a key, or is fit to be one key only, into as many keys as an application needs. Two people who agree on a shared secret by Diffie-Hellman get a point of an elliptic curve, whose bytes are not uniformly random; a password manager has one master key and needs a key per vault, per device, per purpose. Using the same key for two purposes, encryption and authentication for example, can let an attack on one break the other; using a raw Diffie-Hellman output as an AES key wastes part of its strength. HKDF fixes both: it concentrates the entropy of its input into a pseudorandom key, then expands it into independent keys, one per label. BLAKE2b subkeys, libsodium’s crypto_kdf, split a master key that is already uniformly random into keys numbered by id. PBKDF2 is the older answer to another problem, a key from a password, which Argon2id now answers better (Password hashing). Standards and formats that predate HKDF, or were written for NIST’s validations, name their own derivations: Kerberos and NIST SP 800-108’s KBKDF, JOSE’s ECDH-ES and NIST SP 800-56C’s one-step KDF, ECIES and ANSI X9.63’s KDF (Key derivations of standards).

The key derivations are the functions of hash that run on a backend, a C library or Boost.Hash2, that the program names or leaves to the default, backends::hash2 (The default backend); BLAKE2b subkeys run on libsodium alone, and the key derivations of standards on OpenSSL alone, which is never a default: the call names it. Each backend gives the same bytes for the same inputs: the tests check them against each other on random inputs on every target.

HKDF

HKDF (RFC 5869, 2010, Krawczyk) has two steps, both HMACs. Extract takes an optional salt and the input keying material (IKM) and returns a pseudorandom key (PRK) of the hmac’s digest size: PRK = HMAC(salt, IKM). Expand takes the PRK and an info string, the label of one purpose, and returns up to 255 digests of output, each block an HMAC of the previous block, the info and a counter. hkdf does both; hkdf_extract and hkdf_expand do one each, for a protocol that names a step, or a program that extracts once and expands many times. TLS 1.3, Signal, WireGuard, Noise and Nostr’s NIP-44 derive their keys with it.

This section adapts the guidance of libsodium’s documentation on HKDF (key_derivation/hkdf.md of libsodium-doc, ISC licence, kept in NOTICE.md), in hash’s own terms.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hkdf.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    // RFC 5869, appendix A.1.
    auto const ikm = example::from_hex("0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b");
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c");
    auto const info = example::from_hex("f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9");

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 42> okm{};
    auto done = webcpp::hash::hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(okm, salt, ikm, info);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "okm " << example::hex(okm) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(okm) !=
        "3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865") {
        return 1;
    }

    // The two steps of HKDF apart: extract turns the input into a uniform pseudorandom key, and
    // expand stretches it to the length asked, once per context. A program that needs several
    // keys from one secret extracts once and expands as many times as it needs.
    auto prk = webcpp::hash::hkdf_extract<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(salt, ikm);
    if (!prk) {
        std::cerr << prk.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 42> again{};
    done = webcpp::hash::hkdf_expand<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(again, *prk, info);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "two steps " << (again == okm ? "same" : "different") << '\n';

    // The use: one shared secret, two keys. Each key has its own info, so that the encryption
    // key and the authentication key are independent: a key used for two purposes can let an
    // attack on one purpose break the other. The secret is already uniform (a key agreement's
    // output hashed, say), so an empty salt is fine.
    auto const secret =
        example::from_hex("202122232425262728292a2b2c2d2e2f303132333435363738393a3b3c3d3e3f");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> encryption{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> authentication{};
    done = webcpp::hash::hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(
        encryption, {}, secret, example::bytes("example chat v1 encryption"));
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    done = webcpp::hash::hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(
        authentication, {}, secret, example::bytes("example chat v1 authentication"));
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "encryption key " << example::hex(encryption) << '\n';
    std::cout << "authentication key " << example::hex(authentication) << '\n';
}
okm 3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865
two steps same
encryption key c6add3f301ce39db35b0e8ddf3f3ffdb4a64797225bfc2a6a8a5f19d8915c4eb
authentication key 29748eb5c5ce61740da229c9ed99cdd82376f9f7951c998b79f4e03c7801b709

Choosing the inputs.

  • IKM is the secret. It may be non-uniform (a Diffie-Hellman result) but must hold enough entropy: extract concentrates entropy, it never adds any. A password has too little; it goes through Argon2id.

  • Salt is optional and public: a random value per session, or a constant that names the application or the protocol (NIP-44 uses nip44-v2). It separates the keys of different applications that might share a secret. An empty salt is RFC 5869’s string of zeros, and fine when the IKM is never reused across applications.

  • Info names the purpose and is public. Each key gets its own info, written so that no two purposes can produce the same string: an application name, a version and the purpose, as example chat v1 encryption. Info is limited to 32,768 bytes on every backend.

  • PRK must stay secret, and hkdf_expand takes one of exactly the digest’s size (invalid_key_size otherwise). A key that is already uniform and of that size, such as 32 bytes from webcpp::crypto::random_device, can be expanded without the extract step.

  • HMAC-SHA-256 is the usual choice. HMAC-SHA-512 gives longer blocks and no practical gain in security; use it when a protocol names it.

Pitfalls.

  • Never HKDF for a password. HKDF is fast by design: a key derived from a password with HKDF is guessed as fast as the password’s digest.

  • One info, one purpose. Two keys derived with the same IKM, salt and info are the same key.

  • The output is limited: 255 times the digest size, 8,160 bytes over HMAC-SHA-256; more fails with invalid_output_size, the output untouched.

Naming a backend

Most programs never name a backend: the call takes the default, backends::hash2, on every target (The default backend). A program names one as the call’s second template argument, to match the bytes of another program exactly, to share a C library the program already links, or to test one backend against another. backend_has_v<Backend, Kdf, Hmac> says at compile time whether a backend has a function over an hmac; a call on a backend that does not stops the build with a message that names the backends that do.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hkdf.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/pbkdf2.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

namespace {

// RFC 5869, appendix A.1, on the backend `Backend`.
template <class Backend>
std::string okm() {
    auto const ikm = example::from_hex("0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b");
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c");
    auto const info = example::from_hex("f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 42> out{};
    auto const done =
        webcpp::hash::hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256, Backend>(out, salt, ikm, info);
    return done ? example::hex(out) : done.error().message();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    auto const hash2 = okm<webcpp::hash::backends::hash2>();
    auto const sodium = okm<webcpp::hash::backends::sodium>();
    auto const bearssl = okm<webcpp::hash::backends::bearssl>();

    std::cout << "hash2 " << hash2 << '\n';
    std::cout << "sodium " << (sodium == hash2 ? "same" : sodium) << '\n';
    std::cout << "bearssl " << (bearssl == hash2 ? "same" : bearssl) << '\n';
    if (hash2 !=
        "3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A backend that does not have the function is a compile-time fact, not a runtime failure:
    // libsodium has no PBKDF2, and asking for it by name stops the build.
    using webcpp::hash::backend_has_v;
    using webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256;
    namespace kdfs = webcpp::hash::kdfs;
    std::cout << "sodium has pbkdf2: "
              << (backend_has_v<webcpp::hash::backends::sodium, kdfs::pbkdf2, hmac_sha2_256> ? "yes"
                                                                                             : "no")
              << '\n';
    std::cout << "bearssl has hkdf: "
              << (backend_has_v<webcpp::hash::backends::bearssl, kdfs::hkdf, hmac_sha2_256> ? "yes"
                                                                                            : "no")
              << '\n';
}
hash2 3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865
sodium same
bearssl same
sodium has pbkdf2: no
bearssl has hkdf: yes

PBKDF2

PBKDF2 (RFC 8018, first published in 2000 in PKCS #5 v2.0) derives a key from a password by iterating an HMAC: each block of output is the XOR of thousands or millions of chained HMACs of the password, so that every guess an attacker tries costs as many HMACs as the iteration count. It needs no memory, which is its weakness: a graphics card or a dedicated chip runs thousands of PBKDF2 guesses in parallel, where Argon2id and scrypt force each guess to hold megabytes. PBKDF2 remains where a standard names it: BIP39 derives every Bitcoin wallet’s seed from its words with 2,048 iterations of HMAC-SHA-512, and FIPS 140 validated products accept it when Argon2id is not approved.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/pbkdf2.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> vector{};
    auto done = webcpp::hash::pbkdf2<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(vector, example::bytes("passwd"),
                                                                  example::bytes("salt"), 1);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "rfc7914 " << example::hex(vector) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(vector) !=
        "55ac046e56e3089fec1691c22544b605f94185216dde0465e68b9d57c20dacbc"
        "49ca9cccf179b645991664b39d77ef317c71b845b1e30bd509112041d3a19783") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A key from a password. The iteration count is the cost an attacker pays for every guess:
    // too few, and a GPU tries billions of passwords a second. In a real program the salt is
    // 16 random bytes per user (webcpp::crypto::random_device), stored beside the result; it is
    // fixed here so that the output is the same on every run.
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    done = webcpp::hash::pbkdf2<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(
        key, example::bytes("correct horse battery staple"), salt, 600'000);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "600000 iterations " << example::hex(key) << '\n';
}
rfc7914 55ac046e56e3089fec1691c22544b605f94185216dde0465e68b9d57c20dacbc49ca9cccf179b645991664b39d77ef317c71b845b1e30bd509112041d3a19783
600000 iterations ef177144eec9420cbc1093d2a8b344a92bc506d0d4ec9c028dd19f8324d8c1e6

Pitfalls.

  • Iterations are the whole defence. OWASP’s Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends 600,000 iterations of HMAC-SHA-256, or 210,000 of HMAC-SHA-512, for passwords; BIP39’s 2,048 protect a seed of high entropy, not a password. Measure the time on the slowest device the program runs on (a phone, a browser tab: WebAssembly is slower than native; The measured data has the measured times).

  • A random salt per password, 16 bytes from webcpp::crypto::random_device, stored beside the result: without it, one guess tests every user at once and precomputed tables work.

  • Ask for no more than one digest. Each further block of output costs the defender the full iteration count again, and the attacker, who checks the first block alone, nothing.

  • Prefer Argon2id for a new design (Argon2id).

BLAKE2b subkeys

blake2b_subkey derives many keys from one master key, each named by a number, the subkey’s id, and an 8-byte context that names the application or the part of it, as libsodium’s crypto_kdf_derive_from_key does. A chat app keeps one 32-byte master key and asks for subkey 1 to encrypt messages and subkey 2 to authenticate them; a backup tool asks for one subkey per archive. A subkey is BLAKE2b (RFC 7693) of the empty message, keyed with the master key, with the id in BLAKE2b’s salt and the context in its personalisation: one fast call, and the bytes a libsodium program derives from the same master key, id and context. It runs on backends::sodium (/third_party//sodium), the one backend that has it.

Unlike HKDF, it does not extract: the master key must already be 32 uniformly random bytes, from webcpp::crypto::random_device or from another KDF. A Diffie-Hellman result or a password goes through HKDF or Argon2id first.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/blake2b_subkey.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;

    auto const master =
        example::from_hex("404142434445464748494a4b4c4d4e4f505152535455565758595a5b5c5d5e5f");
    auto const context = example::bytes("messages");  // exactly 8 bytes

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> encryption{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> authentication{};
    if (!hash::blake2b_subkey(encryption, master, 1, context) ||
        !hash::blake2b_subkey(authentication, master, 2, context)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "subkey 1 " << example::hex(encryption) << '\n';
    std::cout << "subkey 2 " << example::hex(authentication) << '\n';

    // The length is part of the derivation: subkey 3 of 16 bytes is not the start of subkey 3 of
    // 32 bytes.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> short_key{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> long_key{};
    if (!hash::blake2b_subkey(short_key, master, 3, context) ||
        !hash::blake2b_subkey(long_key, master, 3, context)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "subkey 3, 16 bytes " << example::hex(short_key) << '\n';
    std::cout << "subkey 3, 32 bytes " << example::hex(long_key) << '\n';

    // The context is 8 bytes, never padded: a shorter one is refused.
    std::cout
        << "7-byte context: "
        << hash::blake2b_subkey(encryption, master, 1, example::bytes("message")).error().message()
        << '\n';
}
subkey 1 5f5d5836a36db28c61f8533d6b3b43643f2ad29e3366dc8bda85e66c646f13b1
subkey 2 5230c2a58d64ae036b7208a8343f2c108dbd81ed7eefcc5e4c9c73eaae87ca26
subkey 3, 16 bytes 3d332066b096df8f327fe54ecea124e0
subkey 3, 32 bytes d631aa557b76c6a23adc134800f1f4061aebf7daefde67fda855cca356131574
7-byte context: a parameter is outside the function's limits

Pitfalls.

  • The master key is random, never a password. blake2b_subkey adds no work per guess: from a password, derive the master key with Argon2id (Argon2id) first.

  • The context is exactly 8 bytes. A shorter or a longer one is invalid_parameters, never padded or cut, so that two programs cannot disagree on its bytes; spell it as a constant of 8 characters, as "vault v1".

  • One id, one purpose. The same id and context always give the same key: keep the ids in one list, and never reuse one for a second purpose.

  • The length is part of the key. A subkey of 16 bytes is not the first half of the one of 32 with the same id: BLAKE2b’s output size is a parameter of the hash. Lengths of 16 to 64 bytes are accepted, others are invalid_output_size.

Key derivations of standards

Three key derivations are here because a standard, a protocol or a device names them, and a program that talks to it must derive the same bytes: a Kerberos client, a JSON Web Encryption library, an ECIES implementation, a smart card’s secure channel. Each repeats a hash or an HMAC with a counter, block after block, over the secret and a description of the key, as HKDF’s expand step does; none of them extracts first, so the secret must already be a key or a key agreement’s shared secret, never a password. For a new design HKDF is the better choice (HKDF): it is as fast, it extracts, and WebCrypto and every library have it.

They run on backends::openssl alone (OpenSSL 3.5.9’s EVP_KDF implementations "KBKDF", "SSKDF" and "X963KDF"), so a program names it in the call and links /webcpp/hash//openssl, on native, wasip2 and wasip3; none of them has a default backend (The default backend), and a call that names none stops the build with "…​ has no default backend. Name one of: backends::openssl.". The tests check each against OpenSSL’s own test files, NIST’s validation vectors among them, and against a second implementation over Boost.Hash2.

KBKDF (NIST SP 800-108)

kbkdf is NIST SP 800-108’s key-based key derivation in counter mode over an HMAC: from a key-derivation key KIN, each block of output is HMAC(K_IN, [i] || Label || 0x00 || Context || [L]), the counter i written in r bits (32 by default), L the output’s length in bits. The label names what the derived key is for and the context who or what it belongs to (the parties, a session). Kerberos’s AES-SHA2 encryption types (RFC 8009) derive their keys this way, and so do validated modules that must use an approved derivation from a key. kbkdf_options sets the label and the context, and can leave out the separator, L or both and narrow the counter to 8, 16 or 24 bits, for a format that fixes another form of the fixed input; NIST’s validation vectors pass their whole fixed input as the context, with neither.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/kdf_standards.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    auto const base_key = example::from_hex("3705d96080c17728a0e800eab6e0d23c");
    // The key usage 2 in 4 bytes, then 0x99: the checksum key's label in RFC 8009.
    auto const label = example::from_hex("0000000299");

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> checksum_key{};
    auto const done = hash::kbkdf<hash::hmac_sha2_256, hash::backends::openssl>(
        checksum_key, base_key, {.label = label});
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "Kc " << example::hex(checksum_key) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(checksum_key) != "b31a018a48f54776f403e9a396325dc3") {
        return 1;
    }
}
Kc b31a018a48f54776f403e9a396325dc3

Pitfalls.

  • Match every knob of the other side. The counter’s width, the separator and L change every byte of the output: a key derived with L is not the key derived without it. Read the format’s definition, and check one of its test vectors, as the example does with RFC 8009’s.

  • The output’s length is part of the key when L is in the fixed input (the default): 16 bytes are not the first half of 32.

  • The key is a key. A password goes through Argon2id first (Argon2id); kbkdf adds no work per guess. An empty key is invalid_key_size.

  • Approval is the hash’s. SP 800-108 approves HMAC over SHA-1, SHA-2 or SHA-3. kbkdf also takes HMAC over MD5, RIPEMD-160 or BLAKE2, for the formats that use them, and does not stop the build as sskdf and x963kdf do: where an approved derivation is required, pick SHA-2 or SHA-3.

  • Its limits: at most 2r - 1 blocks, and with L at most 536,870,911 bytes (L counts bits in 32 of them), invalid_output_size otherwise; a counter of another width than 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits is invalid_parameters; OpenSSL takes an HMAC key of at most INT_MAX bytes (unsupported_by_backend).

One-step KDF (NIST SP 800-56C)

sskdf is the one-step key derivation of NIST SP 800-56C over a hash, the "Concat KDF" of SP 800-56A: each block is H(counter || Z || FixedInfo), the counter 32 bits from 1, Z the shared secret of a key agreement (an ECDH result) and FixedInfo the description of the key both parties write the same way. JOSE’s ECDH-ES, the key agreement of JSON Web Encryption (RFC 7518), and Kerberos’s PKINIT (RFC 8636) derive their keys with it. It takes SHA-1, a SHA-2 or a SHA-3 (digests::sha1 to digests::sha3_512), the hash functions SP 800-56C approves; another digest stops the build.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/kdf_standards.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

namespace {

// JOSE's fixed info: each field as its 4-byte big-endian length, then its bytes.
void append_field(std::vector<std::uint8_t>& info, std::string_view field) {
    auto const size = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(field.size());
    for (unsigned const shift : {24U, 16U, 8U, 0U}) {
        info.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t>(size >> shift));
    }
    info.insert(info.end(), field.begin(), field.end());
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    // Z, the x-coordinate of the ECDH result on P-256.
    auto const shared_secret =
        example::from_hex("9e56d91d817135d372834283bf84269cfb316ea3da806a48f6daa7798cfe90c4");
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> fixed_info;
    append_field(fixed_info, "A128GCM");  // AlgorithmID
    append_field(fixed_info, "Alice");    // PartyUInfo
    append_field(fixed_info, "Bob");      // PartyVInfo
    // SuppPubInfo: the key's length, 128 bits.
    fixed_info.insert(fixed_info.end(), {0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x80});

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> content_key{};
    auto const done = hash::sskdf<hash::digests::sha2_256, hash::backends::openssl>(
        content_key, shared_secret, fixed_info);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "content key " << example::hex(content_key) << '\n';
    // RFC 7518's "VqqN6vgjbSBcIijNcacQGg", decoded from base64url.
    if (example::hex(content_key) != "56aa8deaf8236d205c2228cd71a7101a") {
        return 1;
    }
}
content key 56aa8deaf8236d205c2228cd71a7101a

Pitfalls.

  • FixedInfo is the protocol’s, byte for byte. JOSE writes each field as its length in 4 bytes and its bytes, and ends with the key’s length in bits: the same fields in another form give another key. Check one of the protocol’s examples, as this one does with RFC 7518’s.

  • Z is the raw shared secret, the x-coordinate of the ECDH result, not a hash of it: an empty one is invalid_key_size.

  • Its limits: at most 232 - 1 blocks (invalid_output_size) and the input the hash takes (input_too_long, past 261 bytes for SHA-1 and SHA-256); OpenSSL takes a secret, a FixedInfo and an output of at most 230 bytes each (unsupported_by_backend).

X9.63 KDF (ANSI X9.63, SEC 1)

x963kdf is the key derivation of ANSI X9.63, which SEC 1 specifies for ECIES and for elliptic-curve key agreement: each block is H(Z || counter || SharedInfo), the same as SP 800-56C’s but with the counter after the shared secret, so the two never give the same bytes. An ECIES implementation derives the encryption key and the MAC key of a message from the ECDH result with it, in one derivation cut in two; smart cards and the key agreements of BSI TR-03111 use it too. It takes SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, the hash functions SEC 1 lists (section 3.5) and NIST SP 800-135 approves for it (FIPS 180-3’s); SHA-512/224, SHA-512/256, SHA-3 or another digest stops the build.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/kdf_standards.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    // Z, the ECDH result's x-coordinate, and the bytes of the sender's ephemeral public key.
    auto const shared_secret =
        example::from_hex("9e56d91d817135d372834283bf84269cfb316ea3da806a48f6daa7798cfe90c4");
    auto const ephemeral_public_key =
        example::from_hex("02d7c5f8f1c5bd2a0a83c0a5b84dbbc1bf1e3b0a8e7dc7cc5b2b8b1d3e8f7a6b5c");

    // 16 bytes of AES-128 key, then 32 bytes of HMAC-SHA-256 key: one derivation, cut in two.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 48> keys{};
    auto const done = hash::x963kdf<hash::digests::sha2_256, hash::backends::openssl>(
        keys, shared_secret, ephemeral_public_key);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "encryption key " << example::hex(std::span(keys).first(16)) << '\n';
    std::cout << "mac key " << example::hex(std::span(keys).subspan(16)) << '\n';
}
encryption key 4ad858e2f9d7a9888c70163e236dc3ba
mac key 5e5694e2c4ac9e60f72587529bb7f0c25e070a32df14a9f3a52e347f4ad1e9fb

Pitfalls.

  • SharedInfo is the scheme’s. ECIES variants differ in what they put there (nothing, the ephemeral public key, a label): read the variant’s definition.

  • Not interchangeable with sskdf: the counter’s place differs, and so does every byte.

  • Its limits: fewer bytes than 232 - 1 blocks (invalid_output_size) and the input the hash takes (input_too_long); OpenSSL takes a secret, a SharedInfo and an output of at most 230 bytes each (unsupported_by_backend). An empty secret is invalid_key_size.

Password hashing

Every service that has a login will one day lose its database, through a breach, a backup left open or an insider. What the attacker then holds is what the service stored for each password, and what it costs to recover the passwords from it is the service’s last defence: people reuse passwords, so a recovered password opens their mail and their bank. A password hash is a function made to be slow and to need a lot of memory, so that every guess costs the attacker time and memory too, on a graphics card as on a server, and a random salt per password, so that each guess tests one user and no table can be computed in advance. The same functions turn a password into an encryption key for a password manager or an encrypted backup.

This chapter adapts the guidance of libsodium’s documentation on password hashing (password_hashing/default_phf.md and password_hashing/scrypt.md of libsodium-doc, ISC licence, kept in NOTICE.md), in hash’s own terms; every function here runs on libsodium by default, and on OpenSSL where the call names backends::openssl.

Argon2id

Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015 and is RFC 9106 (2021). It fills a large matrix of 1 KiB blocks, each computed from earlier ones with BLAKE2b, over a number of passes; an attacker who keeps less memory must compute blocks again, at a cost that grows fast. Argon2id is its hybrid variant, which resists both the side channels of data-dependent memory access (in its first half pass) and trade-offs between time and memory: RFC 9106 and OWASP name it the first choice. argon2id runs libsodium’s by default, with parallelism 1 (one lane), no secret and no associated data; a program links /third_party//sodium. argon2id<backends::openssl> runs OpenSSL’s, with the same costs and the same tag, on native, wasip2 and wasip3 (a program links /webcpp/hash//openssl).

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/argon2.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

int main() {
    // The salt is 16 random bytes per password in a real program, stored with the tag; it is
    // fixed here so that the output is the same on every run.
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f");

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    auto const done = webcpp::hash::argon2id(tag, example::bytes("correct horse battery staple"),
                                             salt, webcpp::hash::argon2id_interactive);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "argon2id " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // A salt of another size is refused before any work, and the output stays as it was.
    auto const refused =
        webcpp::hash::argon2id(tag, example::bytes("correct horse battery staple"),
                               std::span(salt).first(15), webcpp::hash::argon2id_interactive);
    if (refused || refused.error() != webcpp::hash::error::invalid_salt_size) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "15-byte salt: " << refused.error().message() << '\n';
}
argon2id c05ce4c4dd7e0e45ee6011cc59d068ade47df1b01fc0cf9cd4678bdf68a5b7b0
15-byte salt: the salt is not of a size the function accepts

Choosing the costs. argon2id_parameters has two: memory, in bytes, a multiple of 1 KiB, and passes, the number of passes over it. More of either is never less secure; the limit is the time and memory the program can spend.

  • hash gives libsodium’s three presets: argon2id_interactive, 2 passes over 64 MiB, for a login; argon2id_moderate, 3 passes over 256 MiB, about 0.7 s on libsodium’s reference machine; argon2id_sensitive, 4 passes over 1 GiB, about 3.5 s there, for keys that protect very sensitive data and are derived rarely.

  • To tune for a server, decide first how much memory one hash may take, given how many logins run at once (ideally no more than one per core) and the memory the machine is sure to have; set memory to it and passes to 3, and time one hash. If it is too slow, lower the memory and keep 3 passes; if it is fast enough, raise the passes. About one second is the most a login should take; a desktop application that asks for its password once per session can take about five; a job that runs rarely, such as restoring a backup, can take longer.

  • OWASP’s minimum for a login is 19 MiB with 2 passes; libsodium’s interactive preset is above it.

  • WebAssembly is slower than native (The measured data has the measured times), and a browser tab may not get a gigabyte: measure on the target.

Pitfalls.

  • A random 16-byte salt per password, from webcpp::crypto::random_device; argon2id refuses another size with invalid_salt_size.

  • Store the costs with the salt and the tag. Verifying needs exactly the same memory, passes and salt; a program that raises its costs later must know which costs each stored tag used. hash has no $argon2id$ string format: the program stores the three values in its own record (Storing passwords for a login).

  • Compare the tag with webcpp::crypto::equal.

  • The memory is the backend’s. libsodium allocates the matrix with mmap where there is one, else from the C heap; OpenSSL from its own allocator, the C heap; both outside any allocator of the program (What each backend does with secrets and memory). errc::not_enough_memory reports a refusal.

  • Keep the password in memory briefly, and overwrite it when done.

  • Not RFC 9106’s other parameters. Parallelism above 1, a secret (pepper) and associated data are those of the family argon2 (Every parameter of Argon2: argon2).

What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • openssl: OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-ARGON2.pod states that Argon2i’s memory accesses are independent of the data and Argon2d’s depend on it, and states no constant-time property.

  • sodium: libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

The default of argon2id: sodium on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its only template argument (The default backend).

Every parameter of Argon2: argon2

argon2<Variant> is Argon2 with every parameter of RFC 9106, for the cases the function argon2id does not cover: the variant, the passes, the memory, the lanes (parallelism), a secret (a pepper, kept apart from the database, so that a stolen database alone does not let an attacker test guesses) and associated data, in an argon2_parameters. The variants are three:

  • kdfs::argon2id, the hybrid, RFC 9106’s and OWASP’s first choice for passwords. On libsodium it is the Argon2id of the function argon2id, with the family’s parameters.

  • kdfs::argon2i, whose memory access does not depend on the password: an attacker who watches the cache learns nothing of it, but with few passes an attacker who keeps less memory pays less extra time than against Argon2id. It is here to check tags a system already stored with it, such as those of libsodium’s crypto_pwhash_argon2i; new code takes Argon2id.

  • kdfs::argon2d, whose memory access depends on the password: the best against trade-offs between time and memory, but readable through side channels. backends::openssl alone has it, and it has no default: the call names the backend.

The default backend of Argon2id and Argon2i is libsodium (a program links /third_party//sodium), which takes one lane, no secret and no associated data, a 16-byte salt, a tag of 16 bytes or more, and for Argon2i 3 passes or more. The family’s guards are RFC 9106’s; a value they accept that the backend does not take is unsupported_by_backend, before any work, the output left as it was. backends::openssl has every variant with every parameter, on native, wasip2 and wasip3; it is never a default (design D34), so a call names it.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/argon2.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

namespace hash = webcpp::hash;

int main() {
    // The salt is 16 random bytes per password in a real program, stored with the tag and the
    // costs; it is fixed here so that the output is the same on every run.
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f");
    auto const password = example::bytes("correct horse battery staple");

    // The family counts memory in KiB, as RFC 9106 does: 19,456 KiB are 19 MiB.
    hash::argon2_parameters const login{.passes = 2, .memory_kib = 19456};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    if (!hash::argon2<hash::kdfs::argon2id>(tag, password, salt, login)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "argon2id " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // The function argon2id counts bytes: the same costs give the same tag.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> same{};
    if (!hash::argon2id(same, password, salt, {.passes = 2, .memory = std::size_t{19456} * 1024}) ||
        same != tag) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Argon2i, only to check tags a system already stored with it; libsodium takes 3 passes or
    // more.
    if (!hash::argon2<hash::kdfs::argon2i>(tag, password, salt,
                                           {.passes = 4, .memory_kib = 32768})) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "argon2i  " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';

    // Four lanes are RFC 9106's, not libsodium's: refused before any work, the tag untouched.
    auto const refused = hash::argon2<hash::kdfs::argon2id>(
        tag, password, salt, {.passes = 2, .memory_kib = 19456, .lanes = 4});
    if (refused || refused.error() != hash::error::unsupported_by_backend) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "4 lanes: " << refused.error().message() << '\n';
}

argon2i  99c5bc4aca583cd90b6d91947ac4daed7fb7fde6b965a4b74f2417d061a90e6c
4 lanes: the backend does not take this parameter; name a backend that does
#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/argon2.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    namespace hash = webcpp::hash;
    using hash::backends::openssl;

    // RFC 9106, section 5.3: 32 bytes of 0x01, 16 of 0x02, a secret of 8 bytes of 0x03 and
    // associated data of 12 bytes of 0x04.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> password{};
    password.fill(0x01);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> salt{};
    salt.fill(0x02);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> pepper{};
    pepper.fill(0x03);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> context{};
    context.fill(0x04);

    // m counts KiB, as RFC 9106 does: 32 KiB over four lanes, three passes. A password hash takes
    // far more memory; these are the RFC's costs, to check the tag.
    hash::argon2_parameters const costs{
        .passes = 3,
        .memory_kib = 32,
        .lanes = 4,
        .secret = pepper,
        .associated_data = context,
    };

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    auto const done = hash::argon2<hash::kdfs::argon2id, openssl>(tag, password, salt, costs);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "argon2id " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(tag) != "0d640df58d78766c08c037a34a8b53c9d01ef0452d75b65eb52520e96b01e659") {
        return 1;
    }

    // Argon2d (RFC 9106, section 5.1), for uses where no attacker shares the machine.
    auto const argon2d_done =
        hash::argon2<hash::kdfs::argon2d, openssl>(tag, password, salt, costs);
    if (!argon2d_done) {
        std::cerr << argon2d_done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "argon2d " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
}
argon2id 0d640df58d78766c08c037a34a8b53c9d01ef0452d75b65eb52520e96b01e659
argon2d 512b391b6f1162975371d30919734294f868e3be3984f3c1a13a4db9fabe4acb

Pitfalls.

  • Two units of memory. argon2_parameters::memory_kib counts KiB, as RFC 9106’s m does; argon2id_parameters::memory, the parameter of argon2id, counts bytes. The 268,435,456 bytes of argon2id_moderate are 262,144 KiB.

  • Every parameter changes the tag. The lanes, the secret and the associated data are inputs of the hash as the password and the salt are: verifying needs all of them again, so a program stores the lanes with the costs, and keeps the secret where it can read it again.

  • A value RFC 9106 allows may not be the backend’s. libsodium refuses four lanes, a pepper, an 8-byte salt and a 4-byte tag with unsupported_by_backend; check the error, and name a backend that takes the value where one does.

  • Argon2i takes 3 passes or more on libsodium. RFC 9106 allows 1 and 2, which libsodium refuses with unsupported_by_backend: the attacks that trade memory for time against Argon2i are cheapest with few passes.

  • Argon2d is not for passwords. Its memory access depends on the password, which a timing attacker on the same machine can read; Argon2id is the choice for passwords.

  • Lanes are not threads. OpenSSL computes the lanes one after the other, in the calling thread (webcpp builds it without threads): four lanes give the tag RFC 9106 defines for four lanes, in the time of four times the work, not a quarter of it.

  • A secret is a pepper, not a salt. It is the same for every password and kept out of the database (in a key store or the program’s configuration); the salt stays random per password. Store neither with the tag.

  • OpenSSL’s memory on wasm32. m blocks of 1 KiB must fit a 32-bit size_t: at most 4,194,303 KiB, unsupported_by_backend beyond; a WebAssembly runtime may refuse far less, which errc::not_enough_memory reports.

  • The shortest tag. RFC 9106 allows 4 bytes, which OpenSSL produces; libsodium’s shortest is 16. A password hash wants 16 or more.

The default of kdfs::argon2i and kdfs::argon2id: sodium on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its second template argument (The default backend).

scrypt

scrypt (Percival, 2009; RFC 7914) was the first memory-hard password hash: it fills a buffer of 128 r N bytes with Salsa20/8 and then reads it in an order that depends on the data, so that an attacker without the memory recomputes it again and again. Its costs are N (the memory and time, a power of two), r (the block size) and p (the parallelism). Ethereum’s keystore files and many disk and backup encryption tools use it. libsodium, which hash runs, recommends Argon2id unless a format demands scrypt. scrypt runs libsodium’s by default, and OpenSSL’s where the call names backends::openssl (native, wasip2 and wasip3), with OpenSSL’s own memory limit lifted:

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/scrypt.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    // N is the CPU and memory cost (a power of two), r the block size and p the parallelism: the
    // memory is 128 r N bytes, 1 MiB here. A real password hash uses a larger N.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> key{};
    auto const done = webcpp::hash::scrypt(key, example::bytes("password"), example::bytes("NaCl"),
                                           {.n = 1024, .r = 8, .p = 16});
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "scrypt " << example::hex(key) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(key) !=
        "fdbabe1c9d3472007856e7190d01e9fe7c6ad7cbc8237830e77376634b373162"
        "2eaf30d92e22a3886ff109279d9830dac727afb94a83ee6d8360cbdfa2cc0640") {
        return 1;
    }
}
scrypt fdbabe1c9d3472007856e7190d01e9fe7c6ad7cbc8237830e77376634b3731622eaf30d92e22a3886ff109279d9830dac727afb94a83ee6d8360cbdfa2cc0640
#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/scrypt.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> key{};
    auto const done = webcpp::hash::scrypt<webcpp::hash::backends::openssl>(
        key, example::bytes("password"), example::bytes("NaCl"), {.n = 1024, .r = 8, .p = 16});
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "scrypt " << example::hex(key) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(key) !=
        "fdbabe1c9d3472007856e7190d01e9fe7c6ad7cbc8237830e77376634b373162"
        "2eaf30d92e22a3886ff109279d9830dac727afb94a83ee6d8360cbdfa2cc0640") {
        return 1;
    }
}
scrypt fdbabe1c9d3472007856e7190d01e9fe7c6ad7cbc8237830e77376634b3731622eaf30d92e22a3886ff109279d9830dac727afb94a83ee6d8360cbdfa2cc0640

Choosing the costs. OWASP’s minimum is N 217, r 8, p 1, which takes 128 MiB; libsodium’s interactive costs are N 214, r 8, p 1 (16 MiB), and it advises never less than 16 MiB. Tune as for Argon2id: fix the memory the program can spend, time one hash, then trade.

Pitfalls.

  • A random salt per password, the costs stored with the result, and the result compared with webcpp::crypto::equal, as for Argon2id.

  • libsodium’s own limit: N at most 4,294,967,295; hash refuses a larger one with invalid_parameters on backends::sodium.

  • OpenSSL’s own limits: r p below 224 (invalid_parameters), and a password, salt or output of at most INT_MAX bytes (input_too_long, invalid_output_size): its PBKDF2 takes each length as an int. OpenSSL refuses by default a scrypt that needs more than 1,025 MiB; hash lifts that limit, so that backends::openssl computes every cost libsodium does, as far as the memory goes.

  • Memory on Emscripten. The buffer grows the program’s memory past Emscripten’s 16 MiB; /third_party//sodium links with -sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 for it.

What each backend states on constant time, as the capability table read it:

  • openssl: OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-SCRYPT.pod states no constant-time property.

  • sodium: libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

The default of scrypt: sodium on every target, whatever the program links; openssl only where the call names it, as its only template argument (The default backend).

Hashes that are not cryptographic

A hash table, a cache key, a checksum that catches a corrupted disk block and a shard chosen from a user id all need a hash that is fast and spreads its inputs evenly, and none of them needs to resist someone who chooses inputs on purpose. For those uses FNV-1a, xxHash, XXH3, MurmurHash3 and SpookyHash are many times faster than any cryptographic digest. hash re-exports Boost.Hash2’s, and with them hash_append, which feeds a whole value, a struct field by field or a container element by element, to any hash of this page.

FNV-1a, xxHash, XXH3, MurmurHash3, SpookyHash

FNV-1a multiplies and XORs a byte at a time: tiny, slow on long inputs, good for short keys. xxHash32 and XXH64 (Collet) read 16 or 32 bytes per step; XXH64 is Zstandard’s frame checksum. XXH3 is xxHash’s newer design; which of them is fastest on large data depends on the target (Measured size and throughput). MurmurHash3 (Appleby) and SpookyHash V2 (Jenkins) are older hashes kept to read data that already uses them.

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/flavor.hpp>

#include <cstdint>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace {

struct reading {
    std::uint32_t sensor;
    std::int16_t celsius;
    std::string label;
};

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::cout << std::hex << std::setfill('0');

    std::string_view const text = "abc";
    webcpp::hash::fnv1a_64 plain;
    plain.update(text.data(), text.size());
    std::cout << "fnv1a_64(abc) " << std::setw(16) << plain.result() << '\n';

    // hash_append feeds a value's bytes, field by field: the struct's padding bytes are never
    // hashed, and a string's size follows it, so that "ab" then "c" differs from "a" then "bc".
    // The flavor fixes the byte order: the same bytes, and the same hash, on every target.
    reading const r{.sensor = 1000, .celsius = -7, .label = "abc"};
    webcpp::hash::fnv1a_64 fields;
    boost::hash2::little_endian_flavor const flavor;
    webcpp::hash::hash_append(fields, flavor, r.sensor);
    webcpp::hash::hash_append(fields, flavor, r.celsius);
    webcpp::hash::hash_append(fields, flavor, r.label);
    std::cout << "reading " << std::setw(16) << fields.result() << '\n';
}
fnv1a_64(abc) e71fa2190541574b
reading 2319bd4b66f554b3

Pitfalls.

  • Never where an adversary chooses the input. Collisions of every function here can be computed at will: a table keyed by them, filled from the network, is open to hash flooding. Use SipHash (SipHash) there.

  • Never as a security check. A checksum detects a flipped bit, not a replaced file: an attacker who changes the file recomputes the checksum. Use a digest, and a MAC or a signature when the attacker could replace the digest too.

  • Fix the byte order of what is hashed. A struct hashed as raw memory includes its padding and the machine’s byte order; hash_append with little_endian_flavor (or big_endian_flavor) gives the same bytes, and the same hash, on every target.
