Asynchronous calls

Many programs are built around an event loop: a server that answers thousands of connections on a few threads, a browser page, a chat client that keeps its window responsive. Such a program must never wait inside a handler, because every other connection, every click and every animation waits with it. A password hash is made to be slow: Argon2id at libsodium’s interactive costs takes a large fraction of a second, and called inside a handler it freezes everything else for that long, once per login. An attacker who sends many logins at once can then stall the whole service.

<webcpp/hash/async.hpp> gives the functions of hash an asynchronous form in webcpp::asio’s model: each starts the work and returns at once, and its completion arrives later through the event loop, with a boost::system::error_code. Each takes any completion token: a callback, use_awaitable for co_await in Asio, Cobalt’s use_op, use_future. A program names /webcpp/asio//asio in its Jamfile and includes the header by itself: <webcpp/hash.hpp> leaves it out, so that a program without an event loop does not build webcpp::asio.

The functions come in two kinds:

  • The heavy functions, async_argon2id, async_argon2, async_scrypt and async_pbkdf2, run the work on another thread, on an executor the program gives (the executor of a webcpp::asio::thread_pool), and complete on the event loop. They exist only where the build has threads.

  • The cheap functions, async_digest, async_hmac and async_hkdf, cost microseconds: they run at once and complete through the event loop, never inside the call. They exist on every target, for the algorithms the browser’s WebCrypto has (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, and HMAC and HKDF over them), so that a program written once against WebCrypto’s family builds and runs everywhere.

Each runs, by default, on the synchronous function’s backend (The default backend): backends::webcrypto, the browser’s WebCrypto, is used only when the type names it, on Emscripten (WebCrypto in the browser).

The heavy functions on another thread

The program keeps a thread pool for the slow work, and binds the completion to its event loop with bind_executor, so that the handler runs on the loop’s thread. Here a timer of 1 ms on the loop fires while an Argon2id of 64 MiB runs on the pool:

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/argon2.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/async.hpp>

#include <webcpp/asio/bind_executor.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/steady_timer.hpp>
#include <webcpp/asio/thread_pool.hpp>

#include <boost/system/error_code.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f");
    auto const password = example::bytes("correct horse battery staple");

    webcpp::asio::io_context loop;
    webcpp::asio::thread_pool pool(1);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag{};
    bool ticked = false;

    // The work runs on the pool's thread; bind_executor brings the completion back to the loop's.
    webcpp::hash::async_argon2id(
        pool.get_executor(), tag, password, salt, webcpp::hash::argon2id_interactive,
        webcpp::asio::bind_executor(loop.get_executor(), [&](boost::system::error_code code) {
            if (code) {
                std::cerr << code.message() << '\n';
                return;
            }
            std::cout << "argon2id " << example::hex(tag) << '\n';
            std::cout << "the loop ran meanwhile: " << (ticked ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
        }));

    webcpp::asio::steady_timer timer(loop, std::chrono::milliseconds(1));
    timer.async_wait([&](boost::system::error_code code) { ticked = !code; });
    loop.run();  // lint-run: the program's event loop
    pool.join();
}
argon2id c05ce4c4dd7e0e45ee6011cc59d068ade47df1b01fc0cf9cd4678bdf68a5b7b0
the loop ran meanwhile: yes

The function checks its guards first, as argon2id does; a refusal (for async_argon2id, a salt of another size than 16 bytes) is posted to the handler’s executor with its error, and nothing waits for the pool. Then the work runs on a thread of the pool, and the completion is dispatched to the handler’s associated executor; while the operation is pending, the event loop has work, so its run does not return early. The result is the synchronous function’s, byte for byte.

Where the build has threads, WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_THREADS is defined:

Target The heavy functions

Native

Always: every native build has threads, b2’s default threading=single included. A program that must never start work on another thread defines WEBCPP_HASH_NO_THREADS.

Emscripten

With -pthread, which b2’s threading=multi adds: each thread of the pool is a Web Worker. A page needs cross-origin isolation for workers to share memory (MDN, SharedArrayBuffer’s security requirements); under node they run as they are. A program that blocks its main thread (run, join) links -sPTHREAD_POOL_SIZE=<n> so that the workers start before it blocks. The completion reaches the page’s thread through the handler’s executor: an io_context run there, or the executor of webcpp::asio::browser::main_thread_context, whose handlers run as browser callbacks (bind it with bind_executor; the handler must not run an io_context itself).

wasip2, wasip3

Never: wasip2 has no threads, and wasip3’s threads are cooperative, so the work would still block the loop. Call the synchronous function.

Without threads each name still exists, as a template whose call stops the build with "webcpp::hash: async_argon2id runs on another thread and needs a build with threads (…​). Without threads, call argon2id.", so that a program never blocks its loop under an asynchronous name.

Pitfalls.

  • The spans are the caller’s until the completion. The output, the password and the salt are read and written on the pool’s thread after the call has returned: keep them alive, and do not touch the output, until the handler runs. The parameters are copied.

  • Bind the completion to the loop. Without bind_executor the handler runs on the pool’s thread, by Asio’s rule (the handler’s associated executor, else the one the call was given); code that touches the loop’s state from there races with it.

  • Cancellation does not interrupt the work. A cancellation through the handler’s slot before the work starts completes at once with operation_aborted, even when every thread of the pool is busy, and the work never runs (on the handler’s executor: a handler not bound to the loop’s completes on the pool, and so waits for one of its threads); after it starts, a terminal or partial cancellation lets the work run to its end (libsodium cannot be interrupted), then the output is zeroed and the completion is operation_aborted; a total one is then ignored, since zeroing the output is a side effect. The completion runs on the handler’s associated executor, and the signal is emitted there too, as Asio’s slots require: bind the loop’s executor with bind_executor and emit from the loop, never from another thread. The signal must outlive the call until its handler is called or destroyed: the operation clears its slot then, so declare the signal before the io_context and the pool, which are then destroyed first.

  • A call that never completes destroys its handler. A pool destroyed with the work still queued, or an event loop destroyed with the completion queued, destroys the handler without calling it and gives its storage back, as Asio does for any operation: a use_future future then reports a broken promise.

  • A pool sized for the costs. Each Argon2id holds its memory on its thread until it ends: a pool of n threads can hold n times the memory at once. Size the pool to the memory the program may spend, not to the number of logins.

  • use_future without exceptions. An error completes a future with an exception; a program built without exceptions reads errors with a callback or as_tuple.

  • The storage is the handler’s. The operation’s state and its completion are allocated with the handler’s associated allocator (bind_allocator), as every Asio operation’s are, and all of it is given back before the handler runs, a cancellation’s completion included; the pool allocates the job it queues as Asio does. webcpp’s own code calls neither operator new nor the C allocator.

The cheap functions through the event loop

async_digest, async_hmac and async_hkdf run the synchronous function at once, its guards first, and post the completion, with its error code, to the executor the call gives, whence it reaches the handler’s associated executor. The completion never runs inside the call, so a handler written for the browser’s WebCrypto, which always completes later, behaves the same on every target:

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/async.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>

#include <boost/system/error_code.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto const ikm = example::from_hex("0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b");
    auto const salt = example::from_hex("000102030405060708090a0b0c");
    auto const info = example::from_hex("f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9");

    webcpp::asio::io_context loop;
    // The spans are the program's until the completion: okm and the inputs outlive the loop's run.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 42> okm{};
    bool returned = false;
    webcpp::hash::async_hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(
        loop.get_executor(), okm, salt, ikm, info, [&](boost::system::error_code code) {
            if (code) {
                std::cerr << code.message() << '\n';
                return;
            }
            std::cout << "okm " << example::hex(okm) << '\n';
            std::cout << "completed after the call returned: " << (returned ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
        });
    returned = true;
    loop.run();  // lint-run: the program's event loop
}
okm 3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865
completed after the call returned: yes

async_hmac takes a Boost.Hash2 hmac, as async_hkdf does (async_hmac<hmac_sha2_256>), and computes the tag of mac<macs::hmac<digests::sha2_256>>. A digest or an hmac WebCrypto lacks, as async_digest<digests::blake2b>, stops the build: a post would add nothing to the synchronous function.

Pitfalls.

  • The storage is the handler’s. The post allocates with the handler’s associated allocator (bind_allocator), as every Asio operation does; a program that counts or pools its allocations binds its own.

  • The same spans rule. The output and the inputs are the caller’s until the completion, even though the work runs before the call returns: a backend named in the type may run later (WebCrypto does).

  • backends::webcrypto is for Emscripten. Named off Emscripten, it stops the build: "webcpp::hash: backends::webcrypto exists only on Emscripten: name a synchronous backend, or leave the default." In a synchronous function it stops the build on every target, naming the asynchronous function to call.

WebCrypto in the browser

Every browser, and node, has a cryptography library of its own, the Web Cryptography API (crypto.subtle, W3C), usually called WebCrypto. It computes SHA-1 and SHA-2 digests, HMAC, HKDF and PBKDF2 in the browser’s native code, off the page’s thread, and answers with a JavaScript promise. A program built with Emscripten reaches it as backends::webcrypto, named in the type of an asynchronous function: nothing of it is compiled into the program, and a PBKDF2 of 600,000 iterations, the work of a login, runs while the page keeps drawing. It is never a default: the same call without it runs the synchronous default backend (The default backend), the same bytes on every target.

A password manager in the browser derives the key of its vault from the master password, then hashes a file from the key’s handler, each completion arriving through the page’s event loop:

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/async.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/backends/webcrypto.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <webcpp/asio/io_context.hpp>

#include <boost/system/error_code.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    using webcpp::hash::backends::webcrypto;
    webcpp::asio::io_context loop;

    // The spans are the program's until the completion: they outlive the loop's run.
    auto const password = example::bytes("correct horse battery staple");
    auto const salt = example::bytes("per-user salt 01");
    auto const file = example::bytes("abc");
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> vault_key{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> id{};

    // The vault's key first; the file's hash once the key is there, from the key's handler.
    webcpp::hash::async_pbkdf2<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256, webcrypto>(
        loop.get_executor(), vault_key, password, salt, 600000,
        [&](boost::system::error_code code) {
            if (code) {
                std::cerr << code.message() << '\n';
                return;
            }
            std::cout << "vault key " << example::hex(vault_key) << '\n';
            webcpp::hash::async_digest<webcpp::hash::digests::sha2_256, webcrypto>(
                loop.get_executor(), id, file, [&](boost::system::error_code hashed) {
                    if (hashed) {
                        std::cerr << hashed.message() << '\n';
                        return;
                    }
                    std::cout << "file id " << example::hex(id) << '\n';
                });
        });

    loop.run();  // lint-run: the program's event loop
}
vault key 5010a1c238101d3c7c8b0902a0710234ea5b4853e8776a4b2ef586bb1aa35640
file id ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad

Each function checks the synchronous function’s guards first, then WebCrypto’s own limits, then the executor; a refusal is posted to the handler’s executor, the output untouched. Then it calls WebCrypto through emscripten::val (digest; or importKey, then sign or deriveBits) and awaits each promise with webcpp::asio’s browser::async_await, which keeps the operation alive until the promise settles; its bridge to JavaScript takes one block from the C library per promise, outside the handler’s allocator (Allocation). The completion copies the browser’s bytes into the output; a rejected promise, a result of another size, and a JavaScript runtime without WebCrypto are backend_failure, the output zeroed. Include <webcpp/hash/backends/webcrypto.hpp> or <webcpp/hash/async.hpp>: each brings the other.

Pitfalls.

  • The executor is the page’s io_context. The promise settles in the JavaScript event loop, and only an io_context run on the calling thread returns to it while it waits. Given the executor of a thread_pool, whose threads never return to it, the call would never complete: the build stops, or, behind any_io_executor, the call completes with invalid_parameters. Strands and type-erased executors of the io_context are accepted; behind any_io_executor, one rebound to another allocator, or a strand of a strand (make_strand(make_strand(executor))), is not, since the erasure hides its type: pass the inner strand, or the executor of the io_context. That the io_context runs on the calling thread is the program’s duty: it cannot be checked.

  • WebCrypto’s limits are narrower. An HKDF info longer than 1,024 bytes (node’s limit, where the other backends take 32,768) completes with input_too_long; PBKDF2’s iteration count is at most 2^32 - 1 (invalid_iterations); an output of HKDF or PBKDF2 is at most (2^32 - 1) / 8 bytes. A program that needs more names a synchronous backend.

  • An empty HMAC key is one zero byte. WebCrypto refuses an empty key; HMAC pads every key with zeros to its block (RFC 2104), so the two are the same key, and webcpp passes one zero byte: the tag is the other backends’.

  • A short tag is the tag cut. async_hmac takes a tag of 10 bytes up to the digest’s size, as mac does; WebCrypto computes the whole tag and the output keeps its first bytes.

  • Cancellation does not stop the browser. A terminal or partial cancellation through the handler’s slot completes at once with operation_aborted, the output zeroed; the browser’s work still runs to its end, and its result is dropped. A total one is not honoured.

  • The spans are the caller’s until the completion. The browser reads a copy of the inputs, made when each call starts, and the output is written in the completion.

Use case: a peer-to-peer network

In a peer-to-peer network, a file-sharing app, a social protocol such as Nostr, a sync engine between devices, nobody is trusted: every peer may lie, replay or flood. Hashes are what make that workable. A piece of content named by its digest cannot be swapped by the peer that serves it; an event named by its digest cannot be altered by the relay that forwards it; two peers that agree on a secret derive their keys from it without a server; and a node that keeps tables of what peers send it keeps them in shape when a peer sends thousands of crafted keys. This chapter builds each of those from hash’s primitives.

The steps that a protocol defines (Nostr’s serialization, NIP-44’s labels) are shown as what a domain library, webcpp::nostr for example, would build from these primitives; hash has no such function. JavaScript applications do the same with paulmillr’s noble libraries: the Nostr client library nostr-tools computes event ids and NIP-44 keys with @noble/hashes. The code below is webcpp’s own.

Content addressing

The problem. A file-sharing app fetches the pieces of a file from peers it does not know. A peer that sends a corrupted or malicious piece must be caught before the piece is used.

The idea. Name the content by its digest. The name is published by whoever created the content; anybody who receives the bytes hashes them and compares: a single changed bit gives another name. BLAKE3 suits it best: its tree lets a receiver verify a large file part by part, and natively it is the fastest cryptographic digest measured here (Measured size and throughput). SHA-256 is the choice where a format names it, as Git and IPFS’s default CIDs do.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/blake3.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace {

// The id of a file: its BLAKE3 hash, fed in chunks as a program reads a file, so that a file
// of any size is hashed with the memory of one chunk.
std::string id_of(std::span<std::uint8_t const> content) {
    constexpr std::size_t chunk = std::size_t{64} * 1024;
    webcpp::hash::blake3 hash;
    for (std::size_t offset = 0; offset < content.size(); offset += chunk) {
        auto const piece = content.subspan(offset, std::min(chunk, content.size() - offset));
        hash.update(piece.data(), piece.size());
    }
    return example::hex(hash.result());
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> content(102400);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < content.size(); ++i) {
        content[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i % 251);
    }

    // The sender publishes the id; the content may come from anywhere.
    auto const id = id_of(content);
    std::cout << "id " << id << '\n';
    if (id != "bc3e3d41a1146b069abffad3c0d44860cf664390afce4d9661f7902e7943e085") {
        return 1;
    }

    // A receiver recomputes the id of what it got. The id is public, not a secret, so an
    // ordinary comparison is right here. One flipped byte gives an unrelated id.
    std::cout << "intact " << (id_of(content) == id ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
    content[5000] ^= 1U;
    std::cout << "corrupted " << (id_of(content) == id ? "undetected" : "detected") << '\n';
}
id bc3e3d41a1146b069abffad3c0d44860cf664390afce4d9661f7902e7943e085
intact yes
corrupted detected

Mistakes. A digest of 64 bits or of a non-cryptographic hash lets a peer craft a piece with the same name; keep 256 bits. Hash the bytes as they will be used, after decompression or parsing, or a peer sends two encodings of different content with one name. The name protects the content, not its freshness: a peer can still serve an old version under its old name, which the application solves by signing the list of current names.

Nostr event ids

The problem. A Nostr event travels through relays its author does not control. A relay that changes the content, the time or the tags of an event must be caught.

The idea. NIP-01 defines the event’s id as the SHA-256 of a canonical serialization, the JSON array [0, pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content] written with no whitespace and with fixed escaping, and the author signs the id with a BIP340 Schnorr signature (webcpp::crypto’s secp256k1). Any reader recomputes the id from the fields it received and checks the signature over it. The serialization is the protocol’s, a domain library’s job; the digest is hash’s sha2_256.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace {

// NIP-01 escapes the line feed, the double quote, the backslash, the carriage return, the tab,
// the backspace and the form feed, and no other character: another escape would change the
// bytes that are hashed, and so the id.
std::string escape(std::string_view content) {
    std::string out;
    for (char const c : content) {
        switch (c) {
            case '\n': out += "\\n"; break;
            case '"': out += "\\\""; break;
            case '\\': out += "\\\\"; break;
            case '\r': out += "\\r"; break;
            case '\t': out += "\\t"; break;
            case '\b': out += "\\b"; break;
            case '\f': out += "\\f"; break;
            default: out += c;
        }
    }
    return out;
}

// The event's serialization for its id, with no tags.
std::string serialize(std::string_view pubkey, std::uint64_t created_at, std::uint32_t kind,
                      std::string_view content) {
    return "[0,\"" + std::string(pubkey) + "\"," + std::to_string(created_at) + "," +
           std::to_string(kind) + ",[],\"" + escape(content) + "\"]";
}

std::string id_of(std::string const& serialization) {
    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 hash;
    hash.update(serialization.data(), serialization.size());
    return example::hex(hash.result());
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::string_view const pubkey =
        "79be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798";

    auto const text = serialize(pubkey, 1700000000, 1, "hello from webcpp");
    std::cout << "serialization " << text << '\n';
    auto const id = id_of(text);
    std::cout << "id " << id << '\n';

    // A content with a line feed and quotes goes through the escapes.
    auto const quoted = serialize(pubkey, 1700000000, 1, "say \"hi\"\nbye");
    std::cout << "escaped id " << id_of(quoted) << '\n';
}
serialization [0,"79be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798",1700000000,1,[],"hello from webcpp"]
id e2946c8a1edeff28566f13d47c72913abf2b7423f7e0e1b58eee87aa5e72889a
escaped id b1038192ec8d1ae60481b6cff249e5c67ca0b17bfc5828921baa753b50d21c4e

Mistakes. Recomputing the id from a JSON library’s own output, whose whitespace, key order or escaping differs from NIP-01’s, gives another id and rejects valid events, or, worse, accepts an event whose id was never checked. Always recompute the id; never trust the id field a relay sends.

Keys between two peers: NIP-44

The problem. Two Nostr users want to exchange private messages. They each have a secp256k1 key pair, and nothing else in common.

The idea. Each computes the ECDH shared point from their own secret key and the other’s public key (webcpp::crypto) and keeps its x coordinate, 32 bytes that both sides compute alike but that are not a uniform key. NIP-44 version 2 turns them into a conversation key with HKDF-Extract over HMAC-SHA-256, with the salt nip44-v2, then expands a key per message with a random nonce. The salt is NIP-44’s name for its use of the secret: another protocol over the same key pair, with another salt, gets unrelated keys.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hkdf.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto const shared_x =
        example::from_hex("c6047f9441ed7d6d3045406e95c07cd85c778e4b8cef3ca7abac09b95c709ee5");

    // The key is the same for both parties of the conversation, whoever of them computes it.
    // NIP-44's later steps (expanding a key per message from a random nonce) are webcpp::nostr's.
    auto key = webcpp::hash::hkdf_extract<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(example::bytes("nip44-v2"),
                                                                       shared_x);
    if (!key) {
        std::cerr << key.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "conversation_key " << example::hex(*key) << '\n';
}
conversation_key c41c775356fd92eadc63ff5a0dc1da211b268cbea22316767095b2871ea1412d

The example’s input is the x coordinate the two peers share when one secret key is 1 and the other public key is 2G; its output is computed independently with Python’s hmac. The message keys, the padding and the encryption of NIP-44 are webcpp::nostr’s.

Mistakes. Using the shared x coordinate directly as a key, which wastes its structure and ties every protocol on the key pair together; hashing it with a plain SHA-256 instead of the HKDF the protocol names, which gives keys no other client computes; reusing one message key for two messages.

Tables of what peers send

A node keeps sets of peer ids, of event ids it has seen, of pending requests, each keyed by values that other peers choose. With an unkeyed hash, a peer that sends ids chosen to collide turns every lookup into a scan and stalls the node. A SipHash keyed with random bytes at start-up takes that choice away: SipHash shows the table, in example/siphash.cpp.

Use case: a cryptocurrency wallet

A wallet app holds keys that move money, and its mistakes are paid in coins that no one can return. Its hashes are not chosen: each chain’s standards name them, and a wallet that computes a seed, an address or a checksum differently from every other wallet sends funds where nobody can reach them. This chapter computes the three steps every Bitcoin and Ethereum wallet takes, from the standards’ own test vectors: the seed from the recovery words, the hash of a Bitcoin public key in its address, and an Ethereum address with its checksum.

Each step is a protocol’s (BIP39, BIP141, EIP-55), and is shown as what a domain library, webcpp::bitcoin or webcpp::ethereum, would build from hash’s primitives; hash has no BIP, EIP or address function. JavaScript wallets do the same with paulmillr’s noble libraries: the Ethereum library viem computes Keccak-256 with @noble/hashes, and scure-bip39 derives BIP39 seeds with it. The code below is webcpp’s own.

The seed of a wallet: BIP39

The problem. A wallet must be recoverable from something a person can write on paper. BIP39 encodes 128 to 256 random bits as 12 to 24 words, with a checksum; the wallet then needs a 64-byte seed from the words, from which every key derives (BIP32).

The idea. The seed is PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512 of the words, normalised to Unicode NFKD, with the salt mnemonic followed by an optional passphrase, at 2,048 iterations. The passphrase makes a second wallet from the same words: someone who finds the paper without the passphrase finds an empty wallet. The word list, the checksum and the normalisation are webcpp::bitcoin’s; the KDF is hash’s pbkdf2.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/pbkdf2.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string const mnemonic =
        "abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon abandon "
        "about";
    std::string const passphrase = "TREZOR";

    // The passphrase goes into the salt, so the same mnemonic with another passphrase is another
    // wallet, and nothing says the passphrase was wrong.
    std::string const salt = "mnemonic" + passphrase;

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 64> seed{};
    auto const done = webcpp::hash::pbkdf2<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_512>(
        seed, example::bytes(mnemonic), example::bytes(salt), 2048);
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "seed " << example::hex(seed) << '\n';
    if (example::hex(seed) !=
        "c55257c360c07c72029aebc1b53c05ed0362ada38ead3e3e9efa3708e5349553"
        "1f09a6987599d18264c1e1c92f2cf141630c7a3c4ab7c81b2f001698e7463b04") {
        return 1;
    }
}
seed c55257c360c07c72029aebc1b53c05ed0362ada38ead3e3e9efa3708e53495531f09a6987599d18264c1e1c92f2cf141630c7a3c4ab7c81b2f001698e7463b04

The words, the passphrase TREZOR and the seed are BIP39’s first English test vector.

Mistakes. 2,048 iterations do not make a weak secret strong: the words carry 128 bits or more of randomness, which is the protection, and a passphrase alone, as a "brain wallet", is guessed. Skipping the NFKD normalisation gives another seed for any word or passphrase with accents. And the seed is as secret as the words: it never leaves the device in clear.

A Bitcoin address: hash160

The problem. A Bitcoin address must be short, and must not reveal the public key until the coins are spent.

The idea. Legacy (P2PKH) and SegWit version 0 (P2WPKH) addresses commit to hash160 of the public key: RIPEMD-160 of SHA-256 of its 33 compressed bytes. The two digests together give 20 bytes, and an attacker would have to break both to substitute a key. The address’s encoding (Base58Check or Bech32) is webcpp::bitcoin’s.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto const public_key =
        example::from_hex("0279be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798");

    // Two functions in a row: the second hashes the first's digest, not the key. Skipping the
    // SHA-256 gives a 20-byte value that no Bitcoin node computes.
    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 first;
    first.update(public_key.data(), public_key.size());
    auto const inner = first.result();

    webcpp::hash::ripemd_160 second;
    second.update(inner.data(), inner.size());
    auto const hash160 = example::hex(second.result());
    std::cout << "hash160 " << hash160 << '\n';

    if (hash160 != "751e76e8199196d454941c45d1b3a323f1433bd6") {
        return 1;
    }
}
hash160 751e76e8199196d454941c45d1b3a323f1433bd6

The public key is that of the secret key 1, the generator point of secp256k1; its hash160 is the one inside the well-known address of that key, and the example’s value is computed independently with Python.

Mistakes. Hashing the uncompressed key (65 bytes) gives another, valid but different address; wallets must agree on the form. RIPEMD-160 alone is legacy: use it only inside hash160, never for a new design (MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD: legacy).

An Ethereum address: Keccak-256 and EIP-55

The problem. An Ethereum address is 20 bytes, typed or pasted as 40 hexadecimal digits. A single wrong digit sends funds to an address nobody holds.

The idea. The address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 of the 64-byte public key (x and y, without the prefix byte). EIP-55 adds a checksum without changing the address: each letter of the hexadecimal form is written in upper case where the same position of the Keccak-256 of the lower-case form is 8 or more. A wallet that receives a mixed-case address checks the case and refuses a typo: EIP-55 puts the chance that a mistyped address still passes at about 0.0247 percent.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/keccak.hpp>

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string>

namespace {

std::string keccak_hex(std::span<std::uint8_t const> data) {
    webcpp::hash::keccak_256 hash;
    hash.update(data.data(), data.size());
    return example::hex(hash.result());
}

// EIP-55: a letter of the address is upper case when the same position of the Keccak-256 of the
// lowercase address (as ASCII text, without 0x) is 8 or more. A wallet that finds a letter in
// the wrong case knows that a character was mistyped.
std::string checksummed(std::string const& lower) {
    std::string const digest = keccak_hex(example::bytes(lower));
    std::string out = "0x";
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < lower.size(); ++i) {
        bool const letter = lower[i] >= 'a' && lower[i] <= 'f';
        bool const upper = digest[i] >= '8';
        out += letter && upper ? static_cast<char>(lower[i] - 'a' + 'A') : lower[i];
    }
    return out;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    auto const public_key = example::from_hex(
        "79be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798"
        "483ada7726a3c4655da4fbfc0e1108a8fd17b448a68554199c47d08ffb10d4b8");

    // The last 20 of the 32 bytes: 40 hexadecimal digits from the 24th.
    auto const lower = keccak_hex(public_key).substr(24);
    std::cout << "address 0x" << lower << '\n';

    auto const mixed = checksummed(lower);
    std::cout << "checksummed " << mixed << '\n';
    if (mixed != "0x7E5F4552091A69125d5DfCb7b8C2659029395Bdf") {
        return 1;
    }
}
address 0x7e5f4552091a69125d5dfcb7b8c2659029395bdf
checksummed 0x7E5F4552091A69125d5DfCb7b8C2659029395Bdf

The public key is again that of the secret key 1; the address is the one every Ethereum tool gives for it, and the example’s values are computed independently with a Python Keccak.

Mistakes. SHA3-256 in place of Keccak-256 (Keccak) gives an address that exists nowhere. Accepting an all-lower-case address without a checksum is allowed by EIP-55, but a wallet should warn: it carries no protection against typos.

Use case: a login and a password manager

Two applications almost everybody uses hold the most personal secret there is, a password: the login of any web service, and the password manager that keeps all the others. Both are attacked the same way, by stealing what they store and guessing offline, as fast as the attacker’s hardware allows. This chapter builds what each stores so that a stolen copy is as costly to attack as possible, and how one key becomes many without one weak use exposing the others.

Storing passwords for a login

The problem. A service must check a user’s password at every login without keeping the password, and a copy of its database must not give the passwords away.

The idea. At registration, draw a random 16-byte salt, compute Argon2id of the password with it, and store the salt, the costs and the tag. At login, compute the tag again with the stored salt and costs, and compare it with the stored tag in constant time.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/argon2.hpp>

#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace {

// What the application stores for a user. Without the costs in the record, the service could not
// raise them later: a login verifies an old tag with the costs that made it.
struct credential {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, webcpp::hash::argon2id_salt_size> salt;
    webcpp::hash::argon2id_parameters costs;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tag;
};

// Without a salt of its own per user, one guess tests every user at once, and two users with the
// same password are visible as such. Without Argon2id's memory cost (a fast hash such as SHA-256
// instead), a GPU tries billions of guesses a second.
boost::system::result<credential> enroll(std::string_view password) {
    credential stored{};
    stored.costs = webcpp::hash::argon2id_interactive;
    auto done = webcpp::crypto::random_device{}.fill(stored.salt);
    if (!done) {
        return done.error();
    }
    done = webcpp::hash::argon2id(stored.tag, example::bytes(password), stored.salt, stored.costs);
    if (!done) {
        return done.error();
    }
    return stored;
}

// Computes the tag again from the salt and the costs that were stored, and compares it with the
// stored one. With == the comparison stops at the first different byte, and the time it takes tells
// an attacker how many leading bytes of a guess's tag are right.
boost::system::result<bool> check(credential const& stored, std::string_view password) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> candidate{};
    auto const done =
        webcpp::hash::argon2id(candidate, example::bytes(password), stored.salt, stored.costs);
    if (!done) {
        return done.error();
    }
    return webcpp::crypto::equal(candidate, stored.tag);
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    auto stored = enroll("correct-password");
    if (!stored) {
        std::cerr << stored.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "stored a " << stored->salt.size() << "-byte salt, " << stored->costs.passes
              << " passes over " << stored->costs.memory << " bytes, and a " << stored->tag.size()
              << "-byte tag\n";

    for (std::string_view const attempt : {"correct-password", "wrong-password"}) {
        auto const ok = check(*stored, attempt);
        if (!ok) {
            std::cerr << ok.error().message() << '\n';
            return 1;
        }
        std::cout << "login " << attempt << ": " << (*ok ? "accepted" : "refused") << '\n';
    }
}
stored a 16-byte salt, 2 passes over 67108864 bytes, and a 32-byte tag
login correct-password: accepted
login wrong-password: refused

What goes wrong without each step.

  • Without a salt, two users with the same password have the same tag, and one guess tests every user; tables of precomputed hashes of common passwords work at once.

  • With a fast hash (SHA-256, MD5) instead of Argon2id, a graphics card tests billions of guesses per second: most human passwords fall in hours.

  • With == instead of webcpp::crypto::equal, the time of the comparison tells an attacker at the network how much of a guessed tag is right.

  • Without the costs in the record, the service cannot raise them later: the record must say which memory and passes made its tag, so that a login can verify an old tag and store a new one with today’s costs.

hash keeps no $argon2id$ string: the record is the program’s, three fields in its own database.

A password manager’s vault key

A password manager, an encrypted backup or an encrypted notes app turns the master password into the key that encrypts the vault. The function is the same, Argon2id (Argon2id), with heavier costs, since it runs once per session: argon2id_moderate or argon2id_sensitive, measured on the slowest device the app supports. The salt is random per vault and stored with it, in clear; the derived key is never stored. Bitwarden, for example, offers Argon2id for exactly this (its documentation is cited in the table of how to choose among the functions of Password hashing).

One key, many purposes

The problem. The vault key encrypts files, authenticates the sync with the server, and names items in an index. If the same key did all three, a flaw in one use (an index that leaks, a sync protocol with a weakness) would expose the others.

The idea. Key separation: derive one key per purpose from the master key, each bound to a label that names the purpose. HKDF-Expand (HKDF) with an info string per purpose is the standard way; BLAKE3’s derive_key with a context string (BLAKE3) does it in one call; blake2b_subkey, libsodium’s crypto_kdf, numbers the subkeys within an 8-byte context (BLAKE2b subkeys). Each derived key reveals nothing of the master key or of the other keys.

#include "hex.hpp"

#include <webcpp/hash/blake2b_subkey.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hkdf.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/hmac.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace {

// The label names the purpose: a key derived for file encryption is unrelated to the one for
// authentication, though both come from the master key.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> from_label(std::span<std::uint8_t const> master,
                                        std::string_view label) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    auto const done =
        webcpp::hash::hkdf<webcpp::hash::hmac_sha2_256>(key, {}, master, example::bytes(label));
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
        key.fill(0);
    }
    return key;
}

// The id numbers the purpose, and the context, 8 bytes, names the application: the same id in
// another application's context gives an unrelated key.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> from_id(std::span<std::uint8_t const> master, std::uint64_t id) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    auto const done = webcpp::hash::blake2b_subkey(key, master, id, example::bytes("vault v1"));
    if (!done) {
        std::cerr << done.error().message() << '\n';
    }
    return key;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    auto const master =
        example::from_hex("404142434445464748494a4b4c4d4e4f505152535455565758595a5b5c5d5e5f");

    std::cout << "hkdf file-encryption "
              << example::hex(from_label(master, "vault v1 file-encryption")) << '\n';
    std::cout << "hkdf sync-authentication "
              << example::hex(from_label(master, "vault v1 sync-authentication")) << '\n';
    std::cout << "blake2b subkey 1 " << example::hex(from_id(master, 1)) << '\n';
    std::cout << "blake2b subkey 2 " << example::hex(from_id(master, 2)) << '\n';
}
hkdf file-encryption 2e509a9b0170c0fa44b7096b1bd400b0d4dcf5bd6a981283b3e4b5587a04acb1
hkdf sync-authentication d4959679ea153ff9c3db06f5665b9f87f9081753b7a3ce0339887a914021df37
blake2b subkey 1 8aa2470393bf13f68beaf081047976653ae18a24f24c74b471fd92dc0d5170eb
blake2b subkey 2 e05c31b8eb3c9bd0a8d0c01010de01e08e42f77b99fa5657fac1623d2fbbbabb

The subkeys of part (b) are the bytes libsodium’s crypto_kdf_derive_from_key gives for the same master key, ids and context: an app whose other half uses libsodium, or a libsodium binding, derives the same keys on both sides.

Mistakes. Two purposes with the same label get the same key: write each label once, as a constant, with the application’s name and a version. Never derive a subkey from a password with these functions: the password goes through Argon2id first, and only the key it gives is split.

Domain separation

The labels above are one case of a general rule: whenever one secret, or one hash, serves two purposes, each purpose puts a distinct, fixed prefix in what it hashes, so that a value computed for one purpose is never valid for the other. HKDF’s info, BLAKE3’s context and the salt of NIP-44 do it for keys; a digest that signs two kinds of messages hashes a type tag first; NIST’s cSHAKE (SP 800-185) builds a customization string into SHAKE for the same reason, and comes to hash with XKCP’s family in a later increment.

Choosing a backend

A digest has one implementation, Boost.Hash2’s or a C library’s. A key derivation has several, its backends: the same function, giving the same bytes, in code of different size, speed and pedigree. A tag of the families (digest_of, hasher, mac, argon2) has a backend per cell of its row, and the tests compute each case on every backend that has it, pair by pair: a thousand random inputs per digest and MAC, a hundred per Argon2 variant, a partial cell refusing exactly what its row says it lacks. A call that names no backend takes the default, which is fixed: no measurement, link or define changes it. This chapter says what the default is and why, how a program names another backend, what each backend does with secrets and memory, and, from the committed data, which backend has which function on which target, and what each cost and allocated when it was measured.

The default backend

Function Default Why

hkdf_extract, hkdf_expand, hkdf, pbkdf2

hash2

the one backend that has every hmac, every operation and every target

argon2id, scrypt, blake2b_subkey

sodium

the first of the order that has them (OpenSSL has argon2id and scrypt too, never a default); a program links /third_party//sodium

a tag of digest_of, hasher, mac and argon2

the first of hash2, xkcp, blake3, sodium that has it

one stated rule: the backend that has the whole of the tag, else in part; none when none of the four has it, and the call names its backend

The families’ defaults follow one rule and never change: the first of backends::hash2, backends::xkcp, backends::blake3 and backends::sodium whose capability table, once increments 2 to 7 have landed, has the tag whole (every option and output size the family accepts), else the first of them that has it in part; backends::bearssl, backends::openssl and the later backends are never a default. SHA-2’s and SHAKE’s default is hash2, Keccak-256’s xkcp, BLAKE3’s blake3, BLAKE2b’s sodium; a tag none of the four has (SM3, Whirlpool, Argon2d) has none, and its call names its backend. Every default has its engine: a program that does not link the default’s library gets the message that names the line to add.

The default is the same on every target, whatever the program links: linking libsodium, BearSSL or OpenSSL makes their backends available to a call that names them, never the default. backends::hash2 is the default because it is the only backend that covers every hmac, operation and target; it is header-only, so a program carries only the functions it calls and shares the SHA code it already uses for its digests; and the differences the reference measurement found for HKDF are nanoseconds natively and a few KB of an isolated program on WebAssembly (Measured size and throughput). No define chooses a default: a program that wants another backend names it in the call, as the second template argument, hkdf<hmac_sha2_256, backends::openssl>; Naming a backend shows a program that does. A backend named in a call that it lacks, or that the program does not link, stops the build with a message that says what to do (When the build stops), and so does OpenSSL on Emscripten. default_backend<Algorithm> names the default at compile time.

What each backend does with secrets and memory

webcpp’s own code allocates nothing and wipes every secret intermediate it holds (HKDF’s blocks, PBKDF2’s accumulators, each keyed copy of an hmac, BearSSL’s context) with stores the compiler cannot remove, on success and on failure. What a C library or Boost.Hash2 does inside its own functions is beyond its reach, and this table says what it is:

Backend Its conditions

hash2

Boost.Hash2’s own temporaries are not wiped: the padded key inside the constructor of hmac and the inner digest of its result(). The digest types, and blake3 and keccak_256, do not wipe themselves on destruction.

sodium

Argon2id and scrypt allocate the memory their costs name, with mmap where the system has it, else from the C heap, outside any allocator of the program; libsodium’s sodium_init keeps its process-wide choice of implementations.

bearssl

hash wipes BearSSL’s HKDF, HMAC and hash contexts before each call returns, and the context of a hasher when it ends. BearSSL’s own temporaries on its stack, the pseudorandom key of br_hkdf_flip, the padded keys of its HMAC and the inner digest of br_hmac_out, are not wiped: they stay in the stack memory of the call until it is reused. BearSSL allocates nothing.

openssl

OpenSSL allocates a KDF and a context in every call, through its own allocator, and frees both before the call returns. It clears the key (HKDF’s IKM or PRK, PBKDF2’s password) and the info when it frees the context; it frees the salt without clearing it. A digest allocates an EVP_MD_CTX and the digest’s own context: digest_of frees both before it returns, a hasher owns them from make until it finishes, is destroyed or is moved from. A MAC allocates an EVP_MAC_CTX and the MAC’s context, which mac frees before it returns. OpenSSL documents that it cleans up and frees these contexts, not that it clears them; its HMAC, KMAC and BLAKE2 MACs clear their copy of the key (the BLAKE2 MACs’ first block, which holds it too, only once the tag is computed), and its SipHash frees its keyed state without clearing it. Its Argon2 and scrypt allocate the memory their costs name from OpenSSL’s allocator, the C heap, and free it before the call returns; Argon2 clears its copies of the password, salt, secret and associated data, scrypt its copy of the password but not of the salt. Its scrypt takes r p below 224 and a password, salt and output of at most INT_MAX bytes (invalid_parameters, input_too_long, invalid_output_size otherwise). Its Argon2 sizes the memory in a size_t: the family argon2 takes at most 4,194,303 KiB on wasm32 (unsupported_by_backend), and argon2id at most 4 TiB less 1 KiB natively (invalid_parameters). Its KMAC takes a key of 4 to 512 bytes, a customisation of at most 512 and a tag of at most 2,097,151, and its HMAC a key of at most INT_MAX bytes: mac answers others unsupported_by_backend. Its KBKDF clears its copies of the key, the label and the context when it frees its context, its one-step and X9.63 KDFs their copies of the secret and the info; kbkdf answers a key of more than INT_MAX bytes, sskdf and x963kdf a secret, an info or an output of more than 230 bytes, unsupported_by_backend. Its first call reads OpenSSL’s configuration file. It holds some lengths in an int, so hash refuses, before OpenSSL is called, a PBKDF2 output (invalid_output_size), a PBKDF2 password or salt, or an HKDF salt (input_too_long) of more than INT_MAX bytes. It is not built for Emscripten.

xkcp

Allocates nothing. KMAC’s keyed state and every hash’s state live on the call’s stack or in the hasher, and are wiped when the call or the hasher ends. A KangarooTwelve hasher keeps the span of its customisation string, not a copy, and reads it at finish (KangarooTwelve (KT128 and KT256)).

blake3

Allocates nothing. Its keyed and derive_key modes hold the key in the object’s state until it is destroyed, without wiping it (BLAKE3).

webcrypto

The browser computes outside the program’s memory, with the asynchronous family alone, on Emscripten (WebCrypto in the browser). Each input (the key, the password, the IKM) is handed to it as a JavaScript copy, and the result comes back as an ArrayBuffer copied into the output: neither copy can be wiped, and each stays in JavaScript’s heap until its garbage collector frees it. The imported key is not extractable. The operation’s storage is the handler’s associated allocator’s, given back before the handler runs.

No backend states that its key derivations run in constant time; the capability table records each upstream’s statement, or the absence of one, with its source, and the matrices below show it.

The measured data

The chapters that follow are generated from data that tests and measurements produce, never typed: the capability table, doc/capabilities.json, renders which backend has each function on which target, over which hmacs, and its constant time and the default of each function; the measured table, doc/measurements.json, the size of a program per backend and target and the throughput of each, a reference measured once, on 2026-11-16, that decides nothing; the benchmark the owner named, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512 at 1,000,000 iterations, its times; and the counting test, the allocations of each C library.

Constant time

What each backend’s upstream states, and where:

  • hash2: not stated. Boost.Hash2 1.92: its headers (boost/hash2/) state no constant-time property.

  • xkcp: not stated.

    • XKCP at d20c8fc: README.markdown, lib/low/KeccakP-1600 and lib/high/Keccak (KeccakSponge, FIPS202/KeccakHash) state no constant-time property.

    • XKCP at d20c8fc: README.markdown, lib/low/KeccakP-1600 and lib/high (KangarooTwelve, TurboSHAKE, Keccak/KeccakSponge) state no constant-time property.

    • XKCP at d20c8fc: README.markdown, lib/low/KeccakP-1600 and lib/high/Keccak (KeccakSponge, FIPS202/KeccakHash, SP800-185) state no constant-time property.

  • blake3: not stated. BLAKE3 1.8.7: README.md and c/README.md state no constant-time property.

  • sodium: not stated. libsodium 1.0.22: its headers state constant time for comparisons (sodium/utils.h) alone, not for its hashing, MAC, key derivation and password hashing functions (crypto_hash_*, crypto_xof_*, crypto_generichash_*, crypto_shorthash_*, crypto_auth_*, crypto_kdf_*, crypto_pwhash_*).

  • bearssl: not stated.

    • BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_hash.h states constant time for its GHASH implementations alone, not for br_md5_*, br_sha1_*, br_sha224_* to br_sha512_* or br_md5sha1_*.

    • BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_kdf.h states no constant-time property for br_shake_*.

    • BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_hmac.h states constant time for br_hmac_outCT alone; mac calls br_hmac_out.

    • BearSSL at 7bea48e (v0.6-39): bearssl_hmac.h states constant time for br_hmac_outCT alone; br_hkdf_* (src/kdf/hkdf.c) calls br_hmac_out.

  • openssl: not stated.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_MD-*.pod, doc/man3/EVP_DigestInit.pod and providers/implementations/digests/ state no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man3/EVP_MAC.pod, doc/man7/EVP_MAC-HMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-KMAC.pod, EVP_MAC-BLAKE2.pod, EVP_MAC-Siphash.pod and providers/implementations/macs/ state no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-HKDF.pod and EVP_KDF-PBKDF2.pod state no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-KB.pod states no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-SS.pod states no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-X963.pod states no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-ARGON2.pod states that Argon2i’s memory accesses are independent of the data and Argon2d’s depend on it, and states no constant-time property.

    • OpenSSL 3.5.9: doc/man7/EVP_KDF-SCRYPT.pod states no constant-time property.

  • webcrypto: not stated. The Web Cryptography API (W3C Recommendation, 2017) states no constant-time property of digest, sign or deriveBits; each JavaScript runtime’s implementation decides, and webcpp reads none.

Measured size and throughput

A reference measured once, on 2026-11-16, that decides nothing: what each backend cost a program on each target, in bytes and in time, when webcpp measured it. Every key derivation’s default is backends::hash2, Argon2id’s and scrypt’s backends::sodium, whatever these tables say (The default backend): hash2 is the only backend that covers every hmac, operation and target; it is header-only, so a program carries only what it calls and shares the SHA code it already uses; and the differences measured here for HKDF are nanoseconds natively and a few KB of an isolated program on WebAssembly. No lane measures these figures again, and a move of a C library’s pin leaves them as they were.

Measured on 2026-11-16 on Apple M5 Max, 18 cores, 128 GiB, Darwin 27.0.0; WebAssembly under wasmtime 47.0.3 (5554cc1a6 2026-07-31) (wasip2, wasip3) and node v26.13.0 (Emscripten). Compilers: native: Apple LLVM 21.0.0 (clang-2100.4.1.1); wasip2: Clang 23.1.0-wasi-sdk (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project 895aa2c896ada719451be2e3673c83da8ddf1141); wasip3: Clang 23.1.0-wasi-sdk (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project 895aa2c896ada719451be2e3673c83da8ddf1141); emscripten: Clang 24.0.0git (https:/github.com/llvm/llvm-project f718ebe873411a562ef6e5c27da36d75b7aaec98).

The native rows hold for Apple LLVM 21.0.0 (clang-2100.4.1.1) on Darwin arm64, stripped with strip; another native toolchain gives other native sizes and times.

Sizes: the bytes of the program built at variant=release optimization=space: natively the executable stripped with strip, on WebAssembly the .wasm file, which carries no debug information. Throughput: the program built at variant=release optimization=speed, run with --time: one computation to warm up, then five timed runs of the workload, each repeated repetitions times; per invocation the median of its five runs, per record the median of its invocations’ medians, with the fastest and slowest run.

Throughput

A hash or MAC in MiB per second over 1 MiB, a key derivation in time per derivation: the median, then the range of its runs, the lower figure first. Per function, the workload:

  • md5_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha1_160: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_224: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_256: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_384: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_512: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_512_224: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha2_512_256: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha3_224: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha3_256: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha3_384: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • sha3_512: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • shake_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • keccak_256: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • blake2b_512: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • blake2s_256: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • blake3: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • ripemd_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • ripemd_160: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • siphash_32: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • siphash_64: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_md5_128: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha1_160: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha2_224: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha2_256: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha2_512: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha2_512_224: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha2_512_256: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha3_224: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha3_256: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha3_384: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_sha3_512: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_ripemd_128: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • hmac_blake2b_512: the MAC of 1 MiB under a 32-byte key.

  • fnv1a_32: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • fnv1a_64: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • xxhash_32: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • xxhash_64: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • xxh3_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • murmur3_32: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • murmur3_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • spooky2_128: the hash of 1 MiB.

  • hkdf_extract: HKDF-Extract of a 32-byte IKM with a 32-byte salt, repeated 1,000 times.

  • hkdf_expand: HKDF-Expand of 32 bytes from a digest-size PRK and a 16-byte info, repeated 1,000 times.

  • hkdf: HKDF of 32 bytes from a 32-byte IKM, a 32-byte salt and a 16-byte info, repeated 1,000 times.

  • pbkdf2: PBKDF2 of 32 bytes from a 16-byte password and salt at 100,000 iterations.

  • argon2id: Argon2id of 32 bytes from a 16-byte password and salt at libsodium’s interactive costs (2 passes over 64 MiB).

  • scrypt: scrypt of 32 bytes from a 16-byte password and salt at N=16384, r=8, p=1 (16 MiB).

PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512 throughput

How long each backend takes to derive 64 bytes by PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512 at 1,000,000 iterations, on each target where the backend exists. The figure that matters to a person choosing a backend is how many password guesses an attacker (or a login) can afford per second, which is the reciprocal of these times.

Measured on 2026-11-15 on Apple M5 Max, 18 cores, 128 GiB, Darwin 27.0.0; WebAssembly under wasmtime 47.0.3 (5554cc1a6 2026-07-31) (wasip2, wasip3) and node v26.13.0 (Emscripten); built with variant=release optimization=speed.

Each case is the median of its invocations’ medians, with the fastest and slowest single run beside it: the spread is part of the result.

Every case derived the independent value (Python’s hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac) on every run; backends::openssl does not exist on Emscripten; libsodium has no PBKDF2, so its row measures its HMAC-SHA-512 in PBKDF2’s loop, written in the benchmark and never part of the library.

Allocation

hash’s own code allocates nothing: no function of webcpp::hash calls the global operator new, on any target, and none calls the C library’s allocator on the targets where a program can count it. Test allocation proves that hash allocates nothing for Keccak-256, BLAKE3, Boost.Hash2’s digests and hmacs, and HKDF and PBKDF2 on backends::hash2, backends::sodium and backends::bearssl, the failing calls (every guard’s refusal) included. It counts every form of operator new and the C library’s malloc, calloc, realloc, aligned_alloc and posix_memalign on glibc, macOS, Emscripten and WASI (on WASI through the linker’s --wrap, which sees the calls of the program and of its libraries but not those wasi-libc’s own functions make to one another); a program cannot count them on MSVC, where the proof is operator new alone. A control allocates once through every form and moves the counter, and the test asserts the exact number of calls made per backend, so a backend that silently dropped out fails. What the counter does not see is mmap, which the C libraries below use.

One exception is not hash’s own: on Emscripten, a call on backends::webcrypto awaits each of WebCrypto’s promises through webcpp::asio’s browser::async_await, whose bridge to JavaScript takes a block from the C library per promise awaited (one promise for async_digest, two for async_hmac, async_hkdf and async_pbkdf2, which import a key first). Test allocation counts a bare await’s blocks, prints them as record operation=async_await, and checks that each WebCrypto call makes exactly that many per promise and nothing more. The table below leaves that block out: it lists the C libraries of hash’s backends, and the block is webcpp::asio’s.

The C libraries are another matter, and the table says so plainly. Their allocations are the library’s, outside the user’s allocator, and hash does not hide them.

  • libsodium’s Argon2id takes its memory matrix (memory bytes, 64 MiB for argon2id_interactive) from mmap where there is one, else posix_memalign, else malloc. The calls the table counts for it are small bookkeeping blocks, not the matrix: the matrix is invisible to the counter wherever mmap supplies it.

  • libsodium’s scrypt takes its 128 r (N + p) bytes from mmap where there is one, else from malloc.

  • libsodium’s first call of a program runs sodium_init, whose allocations are the sodium_init rows.

  • OpenSSL allocates a key-derivation context and its digests through its own allocator on every call; test allocation_openssl replaces that allocator with CRYPTO_set_mem_functions before anything else and counts each call through it. A digest on backends::openssl allocates an EVP_MD_CTX (EVP_MD_CTX_new) and the digest’s context, in each digest_of and in each make of a hasher, and a MAC an EVP_MAC_CTX (EVP_MAC_CTX_new) and the MAC’s context in each mac; the test prints those counts too, and the table below holds the key derivations’ alone. The counts are those of OpenSSL 3.5.9 as webcpp builds it, are measured and never bounded, and change with the version.

The table is generated from measurements.allocation.json by bench/allocation_collect.py, and only from release builds: the counts are those of allocation_release and allocation_openssl_release of bench/Jamfile, the programs of the two tests built at variant=release, and the collector refuses an output of any other variant. The tests of the lanes keep the lane’s variant. The figures are those of the machine the file records.

The code webcpp writes, and what the C libraries do

webcpp’s rule is that it writes no cryptography of its own: every primitive is an audited library’s. hash departs from it twice, by the owner’s decision of 2026-11-14, each time for a construction over an audited primitive, never for a primitive, and each under conditions that its tests and its review hold it to.

HKDF and PBKDF2 over Boost.Hash2’s hmac

backends::hash2 is webcpp’s own HKDF and PBKDF2, written over Boost.Hash2’s hmac<H>, so that both run on every target and over every Hash2 hmac without a C library. The conditions:

  • the code follows each RFC’s text step by step, with the RFC’s step names in its comments, in under 150 lines for both functions;

  • RFC 5869’s seven HKDF cases, RFC 6070’s six PBKDF2 cases and RFC 7914’s two pass, with further cases computed by an independent implementation (Python’s hmac and hashlib);

  • it agrees with every other backend that has the same function on random inputs, on every target where one exists: natively OpenSSL, libsodium and BearSSL; on WebAssembly libsodium and BearSSL, and the browser’s WebCrypto on Emscripten;

  • every intermediate value that webcpp holds is wiped before the function returns, which a test observes wipe by wipe; Boost.Hash2’s own temporaries (the padded key inside the constructor of hmac and the inner digest of its result()) are not reached, and What each backend does with secrets and memory says so;

  • it never compares a secret.

Keccak-256’s sponge over XKCP’s permutation

keccak_256 runs the Keccak team’s XKCP for the Keccak-p[1600] permutation; webcpp’s code does the absorbing, the padding (the byte 0x01, zeros, the byte 0x80) and the squeezing, line for line as Boost.Hash2’s detail::keccak_base<0x01, 512, 256> does. The conditions: Hash2’s keccak_base is the oracle of a test on random sequences of update and result calls, which must give its results; and the type becomes an alias of Boost.Hash2’s own keccak_256 once a Boost release publishes one (Upstream: Keccak in Boost.Hash2), with no change to any result.

What the C libraries allocate

hash’s own code allocates nothing, but two of its C libraries do, outside any allocator of the program, and hash records it rather than hides it:

  • libsodium’s Argon2id and scrypt allocate the memory their costs name, with mmap where the system has it, else malloc (and, for Argon2’s 64-byte alignment, posix_memalign). A program whose memory must come from its own allocator would need the Argon2 reference implementation’s allocation callbacks, a possible later backend; it is not built.

  • OpenSSL allocates its KDF and context in every call, through its own allocator, and webcpp keeps no OpenSSL object between calls, which would be state shared between threads. A digest allocates an EVP_MD_CTX (EVP_MD_CTX_new) and the digest’s context: digest_of frees them before it returns, and a hasher owns them, its own and no other’s, until it finishes or is destroyed. A MAC allocates an EVP_MAC_CTX (EVP_MAC_CTX_new) and the MAC’s context, which mac frees before it returns.

The counting test of allocations proves that hash’s own code allocates nothing, on every backend and target, and measures what these libraries allocate where a program can count it; the measured chapters at the end of Choosing a backend show the counts.

Upstream: Keccak in Boost.Hash2

hash’s keccak_256 exists because Boost.Hash2 has Keccak-256 only under detail: its detail::keccak_base<0x01, 512, 256> is exactly the function, but no public name gives it. This section is the text of a proposal to Boost.Hash2 that gives it one, with Keccak-224, Keccak-384 and Keccak-512, for webcpp’s owner to open as a pull request. When a Boost release has it, webcpp::hash::keccak_256 becomes an alias of boost::hash2::keccak_256, a program no longer links /third_party//xkcp for it, and no result changes, since hash’s sponge is already Hash2’s (Keccak-256’s sponge over XKCP’s permutation).

The proposal

Title: Add keccak_224, keccak_256, keccak_384 and keccak_512.

Motivation. Keccak-256, the Keccak team’s submission to the SHA-3 competition with its original padding, is the hash of Ethereum and of every chain and tool compatible with it: addresses, transaction ids, Solidity selectors, EIP-55 checksums. It differs from SHA3-256 only in its padding byte, 0x01 instead of FIPS 202’s 0x06, and Hash2 already implements both through detail::keccak_base; users who need Keccak-256 today reach into detail or link another library. The four classes below make the existing code public under the names other libraries use (Keccak-256 in OpenSSL’s default provider, keccak_256 in noble-hashes and in Ethereum’s tools).

The change. In boost/hash2/sha3.hpp, after shake_256: a class template detail::keccak_seeded<D> over keccak_base<0x01, 2 * D, D>, with the three constructors every SHA-3 class has (the default, the 64-bit seed and the byte seed, each with the SHA-3 classes’ meaning), and four classes that inherit them, with their HMAC aliases. The seed’s eight bytes are fed little-endian, one at a time, which gives the bytes of detail::write64le without an array.

namespace boost
{
namespace hash2
{
namespace detail
{

// Keccak as submitted to the SHA-3 competition: keccak_base with the padding
// byte 0x01, seeded as the SHA-3 classes are
template<int D>
class keccak_seeded: public keccak_base<0x01, 2 * D, D>
{
public:

    BOOST_HASH2_SHA3_CONSTEXPR keccak_seeded()
    {
    }

    BOOST_HASH2_SHA3_CONSTEXPR explicit keccak_seeded( std::uint64_t seed )
    {
        if( seed != 0 )
        {
            unsigned char byte = 0;

            for( int i = 0; i < 8; ++i )
            {
                byte = static_cast<unsigned char>( seed >> ( 8 * i ) );
                this->update( &byte, 1 );
            }

            this->result();
            this->update( &byte, 0 ); // sets finalized_ to false
        }
    }

    BOOST_HASH2_SHA3_CONSTEXPR keccak_seeded( unsigned char const * p, std::size_t n )
    {
        if( n != 0 )
        {
            this->update( p, n );
            this->result();
            this->update( p, 0 ); // sets finalized_ to false
        }
    }

    keccak_seeded( void const * p, std::size_t n ): keccak_seeded( static_cast<unsigned char const*>( p ), n )
    {
    }
};

} // namespace detail

class keccak_224: public detail::keccak_seeded(224)
{
public:

    using detail::keccak_seeded<224>::keccak_seeded;
};

class keccak_256: public detail::keccak_seeded(256)
{
public:

    using detail::keccak_seeded<256>::keccak_seeded;
};

class keccak_384: public detail::keccak_seeded(384)
{
public:

    using detail::keccak_seeded<384>::keccak_seeded;
};

class keccak_512: public detail::keccak_seeded(512)
{
public:

    using detail::keccak_seeded<512>::keccak_seeded;
};

using hmac_keccak_224 = hmac<keccak_224>;
using hmac_keccak_256 = hmac<keccak_256>;
using hmac_keccak_384 = hmac<keccak_384>;
using hmac_keccak_512 = hmac<keccak_512>;

} // namespace hash2
} // namespace boost

The test, for test/keccak.cpp: the digests of the empty message and of the byte 0xCC are the Len = 0 and Len = 8 entries of the Keccak team’s known-answer files of the SHA-3 competition’s third round (ShortMsgKAT_224.txt to ShortMsgKAT_512.txt); those of "abc" and the HMAC’s were computed with an independent Keccak that reproduces those entries and Python’s SHA-3. It also checks incremental input and the seeds against keccak_base itself.

namespace
{

template<class H> std::string digest( std::string const& s )
{
    H h;
    h.update( s.data(), s.size() );
    return to_string( h.result() );
}

template<class H> std::string digest_in_pieces( std::string const& s )
{
    H h;

    for( char c: s )
    {
        h.update( &c, 1 );
    }

    return to_string( h.result() );
}

void test_published()
{
    using namespace boost::hash2;

    std::string const empty;
    std::string const cc( 1, static_cast<char>( 0xCC ) );
    std::string const abc( "abc" );

    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_224>( empty ), "f71837502ba8e10837bdd8d365adb85591895602fc552b48b7390abd" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_224>( cc ), "a9cab59eb40a10b246290f2d6086e32e3689faf1d26b470c899f2802" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_224>( abc ), "c30411768506ebe1c2871b1ee2e87d38df342317300a9b97a95ec6a8" );

    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_256>( empty ), "c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_256>( cc ), "eead6dbfc7340a56caedc044696a168870549a6a7f6f56961e84a54bd9970b8a" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_256>( abc ), "4e03657aea45a94fc7d47ba826c8d667c0d1e6e33a64a036ec44f58fa12d6c45" );

    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_384>( empty ), "2c23146a63a29acf99e73b88f8c24eaa7dc60aa771780ccc006afbfa8fe2479b2dd2b21362337441ac12b515911957ff" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_384>( cc ), "1b84e62a46e5a201861754af5dc95c4a1a69caf4a796ae405680161e29572641f5fa1e8641d7958336ee7b11c58f73e9" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_384>( abc ), "f7df1165f033337be098e7d288ad6a2f74409d7a60b49c36642218de161b1f99f8c681e4afaf31a34db29fb763e3c28e" );

    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_512>( empty ), "0eab42de4c3ceb9235fc91acffe746b29c29a8c366b7c60e4e67c466f36a4304c00fa9caf9d87976ba469bcbe06713b435f091ef2769fb160cdab33d3670680e" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_512>( cc ), "8630c13cbd066ea74bbe7fe468fec1dee10edc1254fb4c1b7c5fd69b646e44160b8ce01d05a0908ca790dfb080f4b513bc3b6225ece7a810371441a5ac666eb9" );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<keccak_512>( abc ), "18587dc2ea106b9a1563e32b3312421ca164c7f1f07bc922a9c83d77cea3a1e5d0c69910739025372dc14ac9642629379540c17e2a65b19d77aa511a9d00bb96" );
}

void test_hmac()
{
    // RFC 4231's second case, over Keccak-256 instead of SHA-256
    boost::hash2::hmac_keccak_256 mac( "Jefe", 4 );
    std::string const message( "what do ya want for nothing?" );
    mac.update( message.data(), message.size() );

    BOOST_TEST_EQ( to_string( mac.result() ), "aa9aed448c7abc8b5e326ffa6a01cdedf7b4b831881468c044ba8dd4566369a1" );
}

template<class H> void test_incremental()
{
    std::string const s( 1000, 'a' );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( digest<H>( s ), digest_in_pieces<H>( s ) );
}

template<class H, int D> void test_seeded()
{
    // A seed feeds the hash as it feeds the SHA-3 class of the same size: its eight
    // bytes, little-endian, then a result; a key of n bytes, likewise
    boost::hash2::detail::keccak_base<0x01, 2 * D, D> expected;

    std::string const seed( "\x07\0\0\0\0\0\0\0", 8 );
    expected.update( seed.data(), seed.size() );
    expected.result();
    expected.update( seed.data(), 0 );

    H h( 7 );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( to_string( h.result() ), to_string( expected.result() ) );

    H h0( 0 );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( to_string( h0.result() ), digest<H>( "" ) );

    boost::hash2::detail::keccak_base<0x01, 2 * D, D> expected_key;

    std::string const key( "key" );
    expected_key.update( key.data(), key.size() );
    expected_key.result();
    expected_key.update( key.data(), 0 );

    H hk( key.data(), key.size() );
    BOOST_TEST_EQ( to_string( hk.result() ), to_string( expected_key.result() ) );
}

} // namespace

The documentation, for the reference’s list of algorithms: "keccak_224, keccak_256, keccak_384, keccak_512: Keccak as submitted to the SHA-3 competition, before FIPS 202 changed its padding; Keccak-256 is Ethereum’s hash. Not interchangeable with sha3_224 to sha3_512, whose digests differ."

The evidence

webcpp builds this text against Boost.Hash2 1.92 in its test upstream_keccak, on every target webcpp has: the digests above pass, and webcpp::hash::keccak_256 gives the results of the proposed keccak_256 for every length up to three blocks and for random sequences of update and result, which is what makes the later alias safe. The proposal is the owner’s to open; nothing here is sent upstream.

An index for language models

llms.txt, published beside this page, lists every function of hash with its header, its standard, what it is for, its status, when to choose it and the backends that implement it, each with the Jamfile line and the targets, then every row of Choose by use case, in the llms.txt form: a model that reads it can answer "which function, which backend, which Jamfile line" without reading the page. It is generated with the tables of this page from the same data, doc/capabilities.json and doc/guide.json, by tools/hash/doc_tables.py, whose check runs when the page is built; the two never disagree.

Reference

Every name hash declares, in the namespaces webcpp::hash and its backends and kdfs, from the Doc Comments of its headers: each class, function, type and enumerator with its declaration, what it does, what it asks of its caller and how it fails. The other sections teach the library; this one is where a name is looked up.

Macros

Name Description

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_BEARSSL

Defined by /third_party//bearssl when the program links BearSSL; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself.

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_BLAKE3

Defined by /third_party//blake3 when the program links the BLAKE3 C implementation; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself.

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_OPENSSL

Defined by /webcpp/hash//openssl when the program links OpenSSL; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself. Refused on Emscripten, where OpenSSL is not built.

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_SODIUM

Defined by /third_party//sodium when the program links libsodium; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself.

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_THREADS

Defined where the heavy functions of <webcpp/hash/async.hpp> (async_argon2id, async_argon2, async_scrypt, async_pbkdf2 on a synchronous backend) run on another thread: natively, where Boost.Config’s BOOST_HAS_THREADS is defined (every native build, b2’s threading=single included), and on Emscripten built with -pthread (b2’s threading=multi); never on wasip2 or wasip3, whose cooperative threads do not run in parallel. Without it each of those names refuses at compile time.

WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_XKCP

Defined by /third_party//xkcp when the program links XKCP; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself.

WEBCPP_HASH_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when webcpp::hash is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone.

WEBCPP_HASH_NO_THREADS

Defined by the developer to leave WEBCPP_HASH_HAS_THREADS undefined in a build that has threads: the heavy functions of <webcpp/hash/async.hpp> then refuse at compile time, so that no call of the program can start a thread’s work.

WEBCPP_HASH_WEBASSEMBLY

Defined on the WebAssembly targets, wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten.
